q: B3 rated power is -15.7 dBm. B1 is -16.7 dBm. Why is B3 stronger?
a: B3 (1842 MHz) band combiner has less insertion loss than B1 (2140 MHz) because loss increases with frequency in passive components. So B3 arrives at the SMA with less cable/combiner loss, appearing stronger.

q: ACLR measures -55 dBc. What does that mean in watts if carrier is -16.7 dBm?
a: Carrier: -16.7 dBm = 21.4 μW. Adjacent channel leakage: -16.7 - 55 = -71.7 dBm = 0.068 nW. The adjacent channel gets only 1/355,000 of the wanted power. That's a good ACLR.

q: Someone says 'I need 3 dB more power'. What does that mean?
a: They need to double the output power. 3 dB = factor of 2. So if current power is 20W, they need 40W.

q: Your cable shows VSWR of 2.0. How much power is reflected?
a: VSWR=2.0 → Γ=0.33 → Reflected fraction = |Γ|² = 0.11 = 11%. For B1 at -16.7dBm, reflected power = -16.7 - 9.5 = -26.2dBm.

q: Why does a λ/4 open stub act as a short circuit?
a: At the open end, voltage is maximum, current is zero. After travelling λ/4, the wave has shifted 90° in phase. At the input, current is maximum and voltage is zero — that's a short circuit. This is used in bandstop filters and bias tees.

q: Why do you always check cable connections before blaming the DUT?
a: A bad connection adds return loss that looks like reduced DUT output. 1dB of extra cable loss = 1dB deficit in channel power. Always VSWR-check cables first, then troubleshoot the DUT.

q: Why does the RCT measure at BOB SMA instead of the antenna port?
a: Repeatable: cable loss is calibrated. Safe: antenna RF would damage EXA input. Practical: you can't access the RF space outside the unit. The BOB gives electrical access to the signal before PA.

q: DPD is showing MISALIGNED. What do you do?
a: 1. Check observation path cable (OBS port on RFFE → ADC). 2. Check CFR register (0x534020004 = 0xd7). 3. Run dpd-app-orx --debug to see alignment status. 4. If RFFE issue, may need JTAG re-flash (like the RFFE2 LB fault you solved).

q: What is the 9.9765ms delay for B41 TDD?
a: B41 is TDD — the same frequency is used for DL and UL in alternating time slots. The BBU frame starts at t=0. The DL slot starts at t=9.9765ms into the frame. The EXM trigger must be delayed by exactly 9.9765ms to capture the DL burst.

q: RSRP = −95 dBm. Is this good or bad?
a: Depends on context. For coverage design: −95 is OK for QPSK, poor for 64QAM. In your lab RCT: this is typical when injecting at sensitivity edge (−91 to −102 dBm range). Compare to your sensitivity limit: if RSRP < sensitivity_limit, UE can't decode.

q: Your SINR is −4 dB but RSRP is strong. What's wrong?
a: Strong SINR without strong interference usually means very high noise figure (LNA issue) or self-interference. Check if there's LO leakage into the RX path (common if duplexer isolation has degraded). Also check for harmonic mixing products from TX into RX.

q: What's the difference between RSRP from CLI and from OAM?
a: CLI dBFS is raw ADC reading (uncalibrated, relative to ADC full scale). OAM dBm is calibrated (applies gain, DSA, NF corrections). For RCT validation: compare both. They should agree within 1dB after DSA correction. Large difference = ADC_ADJUST register wrong.

q: What is the cyclic prefix and why is 5.21μs chosen?
a: CP is a copy of the end of each OFDM symbol prepended to the start. It absorbs multipath delay spread. 5.21μs was chosen to handle typical urban multipath (500ns to 5μs delay spread) with margin. Rural cells with longer paths use extended CP (16.67μs).

q: Your EVM test shows much higher EVM on outer subcarriers than center. What's wrong?
a: Frequency-dependent gain/phase error across the channel bandwidth. Common causes: cable resonance, filter roll-off at band edges, equalizer not covering full BW. Check: EXA → Modulation Analysis → Subcarrier EVM display. Shows EVM per subcarrier frequency.

q: Why does 64QAM need better SINR than QPSK?
a: 64QAM has 64 symbols in the same IQ plane, minimum distance = 0.155 (normalized). QPSK has 4 symbols, minimum distance = 0.707. For the same noise power, 64QAM has 13dB less margin before symbols overlap and errors occur. SINR must be 13dB+ higher for 64QAM to work.

q: ACLR is failing at −42 dBc (spec is −55 dBc for Metro). DPD shows ALIGNED. What next?
a: DPD is aligned but might not be properly converged. Check: 1) DPD input power (−9 ±1.5 dBm). 2) CFR register (0xd7). 3) Wait 60 seconds after TX start. 4) Check OBS path cable and ADC health. 5) If B41 TDD: verify gate trigger is set or you're measuring in wrong slot.

q: Why does PAPR matter for PA efficiency?
a: PAPR = 8.3dB means the PA must be designed for peaks 8.3dB above average. But most of the time the signal is at average power where the PA is very inefficient (Class AB efficiency at back-off ≈ efficiency × 10^(-PAPR/10) reduction). Lower PAPR = more efficient = less heat = longer PA life.

q: Customer says ACLR was passing yesterday, failing today. Nothing changed. What do you check?
a: 1. DPD convergence status (did it reset?). 2. Temperature — PA linearization is temperature-sensitive. 3. FW version (was there a silent update?). 4. BBU configuration (carrier BW changed?). 5. Cable connections. 6. Compare PreChecks now vs yesterday's log.

q: ACLR upper is −58 dBc but ACLR lower is −48 dBc. What could cause asymmetry?
a: Asymmetric ACLR = problem at one specific frequency offset, not general DPD failure. Common causes: 1) Partial blockage or resonance at that frequency. 2) Mixer spur at that offset. 3) Adjacent carrier from another band at that frequency. 4) Cable resonance. Check SEM for the asymmetric side.

q: You measure ACLR at −42 dBc. The test says FAIL. Your colleague says it was −57 dBc yesterday. What's the first thing you do?
a: Check DPD convergence. A 15dB sudden change almost certainly means DPD is not converged (unaligned OBS path) or was reset. Run dpd-app-orx, check alignment. If MISALIGNED: check OBS cable, wait 60s after TX start, re-run.

q: What's the relationship between PAPR and ACLR?
a: Higher PAPR = more peak events = more PA saturation = more spectral regrowth = worse ACLR. CFR reduces PAPR from 12dB to 8.3dB. This DIRECTLY improves ACLR because the PA saturates less often. But over-clipping (PAPR < 7.3dB) creates its own distortion that also degrades ACLR.

q: PRACH test shows 100% miss detection at all power levels. What's wrong?
a: 100% miss at ALL power levels (including high power like -40 dBm) means the signal is never arriving in the right slot. For FDD: check waveform file matches the configured BW. For TDD B41: trigger delay wrong (should be 9.9765ms). Also check: RU UL path (LNA, cable). Run sensitivity test first — if that also fails, UL path is broken.

q: Why does PRACH use root sequence 32 in your tests?
a: PID32 (Preamble Index/Root 32) is the configured root for your test setup. The ZC sequence root determines which 64 preambles are available. Root 32 is assigned to avoid collision with neighboring cells in production. In lab: any root works — 32 is standard in PW test setup.

q: PRACH sensitivity is measured at −79 dBm. Limit is −82 dBm. What's the verdict?
a: FAIL. Sensitivity is WORSE (less negative = weaker signal) than the limit. The RU needed a stronger signal than specified to achieve <1% miss detection. Root cause: check LNA NF, cable loss, DSA register, OBS path. For certification, this is a hard fail.

q: What does “single DPD” mean on this AAU?
a: One DPD adaptation path (one observation-receiver loop) is shared across the B1 and B3 carriers rather than a dedicated DPD per carrier — the OB coupler feeds a single B1/B3 OB-OUT back to the transceiver. It saves an observation chain but means the DPD must linearise both carriers from one feedback, which is why dual-band ACLR gets the 52 dBc allowance (KPI01).

q: What is the π-PAD for, and why an LPF after the PA?
a: The π-PAD is a fixed resistive attenuator that sets the drive level and improves impedance matching on the TX branch. The LPF after the PA removes the harmonics the non-linear PA generates, so they don't violate the spurious-emissions mask (FC19).
tags: hardware aau rffe tx rx architecture lab intermediate

q: Difference between a gain budget and a link budget?
a: A gain budget accounts for power and losses inside the radio (DAC → cables → PA → circulator/coupler/connector/filter → antenna port) to guarantee the rated conducted output; a link budget accounts for the over-the-air path after the antenna (EIRP, path loss, fading, RX sensitivity) to predict coverage. This workbook is the former.
tags: hardware aau tx rffe measurements architecture intermediate

q: Why reserve ≥6 dB of attenuator margin?
a: The chain gain drifts with temperature (~−3 dB hot) and varies across the band (gain flatness). The variable attenuator needs enough range (4 dB temp + 2 dB flatness = 6 dB minimum) to trim the output back to the target so the radiated power stays within spec across temperature and frequency.

Each step has a quality metric: Symbol Error Rate → Bit Error Rate → Block Error Rate (BLER). 3GPP uses 5% BLER as the sensitivity threshold. The entire DSA framework is calibrating your test to this 5% BLER threshold. Why OFDM was chosen for LTE: OFDM converts a wideband channel into many narrow subchannels (15 kHz each). Each subchannel experiences flat fading (not frequency-selective). Frequency-domain equalization becomes trivial — one complex multiply per subcarrier. Guard bands (cyclic prefix) eliminate inter-symbol interference from multipath. The price: high PAPR (10–12 dB) requiring DPD and CFR. LTE downlink uses OFDMA with QAM modulation on each subcarrier. Uplink uses SC-FDMA (single carrier) to keep UE PAPR low (battery saving). Your RU receives SC-FDMA from UE and transmits OFDMA to UE. q: EXA shows -14 dBm, expected -16.7 dBm for B1. First check?
a: ExtGain setting — is cable loss entered as positive value? If ExtGain=0 and cable loss is 2dB, reading is 2dB high. Connect power meter to same SMA to verify true power.

q: ACLR dropped 15dB overnight — was passing yesterday. First action?
a: DPD reset. Check dpd-app-orx status immediately. A 15dB sudden change = DPD not converged. Was carrier restarted overnight? Wait 60s after TX start and retest.

q: EVM fails but ACLR passes. What impairment?
a: In-band distortion without spectral spreading: IQ imbalance, phase noise, LO leakage, DC offset. These affect constellation quality (EVM) without spilling into adjacent channels (ACLR). NOT a PA/DPD problem — that would fail ACLR too.

q: EVM is 6% on 64QAM but 1.5% on QPSK. What impairment?
a: Modulation-order-dependent: IQ imbalance or phase noise. 64QAM has 4× tighter symbol spacing — same angular error causes bigger relative error. Run TX IQ calibration and check TCXO reference quality.

q: B41 sensitivity fails intermittently — sometimes pass, sometimes fail.
a: Timing issue. PTP phase error fluctuating? ptp4l master offset jumping ±500ns moves the TDD slot boundary relative to your 9.9765ms EXM trigger — sometimes lands in guard slot instead of UL slot. Verify PTP grandmaster is GPS-locked and path delay variation is <100ns.

q: TAE fails — one column 80ns late.
a: 80ns > 65ns. Check: 1) Cable length to that column's SMA (longer cable = more delay). 2) RFFE timing cal for that path. 3) DAC/CFR timing register. Often a firmware issue where one path's digital delay register wasn't set correctly.

q: Why is sensitivity limit better with 4T4R than single antenna?
a: MRC adds 4 branches coherently: signal +12dB, noise +6dB → net +6dB. Already included in your DSA formula.

q: eCPRI link up but no U-plane IQ flowing.
a: 1) VLAN configured on switch? 2) PC_ID mismatch DU vs RU? 3) PTP not locked (RU rejects U-plane without sync)? 4) C-plane: DU sending section descriptors? Check eCPRI counters: rx_u_plane_pkts increasing?

q: Need to check if eCPRI packets arrive at correct rate. How?
a: tcpdump -i ecpri0 'ether proto 0xAEFE' and count over 1s. Expected: ~14,000 packets/s for 20MHz LTE (14 symbols × 1000 subframes × ~1 packet/symbol/carrier).

q: Script works locally, fails on test server.
a: 1) Python version. 2) Dependencies installed (pip list). 3) Absolute vs relative file paths. 4) Permissions on log directory. 5) Network: server can reach EXA IP? 6) Encoding issues with special chars.

q: Which regulatory spec applies to B41 in the US? FCC Part 96 (CBRS) — operation is SAS-granted; your EIRP must not exceed the SAS grant for the CBSD category. Unique to each serial number — cannot use unit 26050509 cal file on unit 26050508. End-of-line testing — fast subset of full RCT:EOL test must complete in Burn-in — catching infant mortality failures:Components follow a bathtub curve: high failure rate early (manufacturing defects), then low steady-state, then increasing at end of life. Burn-in at +55°C for 24-72 hours at full TX power stresses marginal solder joints and components. What would fail in the first month of deployment fails during burn-in instead. After burn-in: another EOL test run to confirm all specs still pass. Root cause: usually CFR threshold changed → larger peaks → overdriving PA. Scenario 2: RSSI accuracy fails only at high temperatureStep 1: Confirm failure is reproducible at +55°C. Step 2: Check TEMP_COMP table in hardware.json — populated? If empty: temperature compensation disabled → RSSI drifts. Step 3: Measure RSSI at +25°C and +55°C with same EXM injection → compute drift = X dB/°C. Step 4: Calculate required TEMP_COMP coefficient. Step 5: Run RSSI cal at both temperatures, update table. Root cause: TEMP_COMP table not calibrated or not loaded at boot. Scenario 3: PA enters protection after 20 minutesStep 1: Which protection? Check fault register: over-temperature vs over-current vs VSWR. Step 2: If over-temperature: thermal camera on PA, check ambient > 55°C, heatsink contact, fan. Step 3: If VSWR: VNA on antenna port — is load present? Step 4: If over-current: check PA bias vs spec, check if unit is over-driven. Monitor temperature over time — steady rise until threshold = thermal compound deficiency. Root cause in 70% of cases: thermal management, not electrical. Scenario 4: Dynamic range fails B3 but passes B1Step 1: Confirm back-to-back with same setup. Step 2: Check ADC channel mapping — correct ADC for B3? (ch 2/3/6/7, not ch 0/1/4/5 for B1). Step 3: Check ADC_ADJUST_B3 — calibrated correctly? Step 4: Sweep EXM −60 to −110 dBm for both bands, plot RSSI vs injected power — compare curves. Parallel but offset: ADC_ADJUST_B3 wrong → recalibrate. Different slope: hardware fault in LNA or mixer at B3 frequency. Root cause: most likely wrong ADC_ADJUST_B3. Root cause: usually missing TX gain temperature compensation. Scenario 6: B41 PRACH detection fails intermittently — B1/B3/B8/B28 all pass B41 is TDD — immediately suspect timing/sync. Step 1: Check DU PTP status — is it LOCKED? Even a brief GPS signal loss can cause PTP to enter holdover. Step 2: Check PTP offset over time — is it drifting beyond ±1.5 μs? Step 3: If PTP is fine: check EXA gating — are you measuring only during UL subframes? B41 PRACH arrives only in UL slots. Step 4: If gating is correct: verify EXM is synchronised to TDD frame — injection must be in correct UL subframe. Step 5: Check fronthaul latency under load — if transport QoS is misconfigured, PTP packets get delayed under traffic → sync degrades → intermittent B41 issues. Root cause: almost always PTP sync or EXA/EXM gating setup. Scenario 7: After PA replacement, ACLR fails but TX power is correct ACLR fail with correct power = PA is on but DPD is not working for the new PA. Step 1: Was DPD allowed to converge? PA replacement resets DPD coefficients — wait 60s after enabling TX. Step 2: If still failing after convergence: the new PA has different nonlinearity than the DPD model was trained on. The DPD coefficients calibrated for the old PA do not match the new one. Step 3: Force DPD re-adaptation — some systems require explicit re-trigger after hardware change. Step 4: Check if DPD algorithm converged at all (DPD_STATUS register). Step 5: If DPD_STATUS shows converged but ACLR still fails: PA bias may be different — check bias voltage matches spec for new PA part number. Root cause: DPD model not re-adapted after PA replacement. Scenario 8: RSSI reads 6 dB lower than expected on one specific column 6 dB is exactly 1 bit in a 12-bit ADC — suspicious of BFP error. Step 1: Is it exactly 6 dB or approximately? If exactly 6 dB: BFP decompression fault (mantissa/exponent mismatch) → check FHGW firmware version, check eCPRI error counters. Step 2: If approximately 6 dB: check cable for that column (swap with known-good cable). Step 3: Run RSSI across all B1 columns — is it only Column X or all columns? If only one column: hardware fault on that column (LNA or cable). If all columns: ADC_ADJUST wrong for that band → re-calibrate. Step 4: Verify ADC channel mapping — is the correct get_rssi N being read for that column? (B3 Col A = get_rssi 2, not 0). Step 5: If column reads correct with EXM at full power but wrong at low power: LNA may be compressed by a strong blocker nearby during the test. Root cause: check in this order — ADC channel mapping → cable swap → LNA health → BFP error. OTA uses anechoic chambers and 3D radiation pattern measurements. The 3GPP spec for device OTA is TS 38.176. Very different from base station testing but shares RF fundamentals. Universal skills — what every company values most:(1) Systematic troubleshooting — find root cause without replacing things randomly. (2) Instrument fluency — set up EXA ACLR measurement correctly without checking manual. (3) Quantitative thinking — think in dB, know what 3 dB means. (4) Automation — write Python SCPI script to automate a measurement. (5) Communication — explain why ACLR matters to a non-RF engineer. These transfer across all companies. Build these first, company-specific knowledge comes with the job. Odd orders matter most: IM3 = 2f1−f2, 2f2−f1; then IM5, IM7…Why it hurts YOUR AAU specificallyYour TX carriers (e.g. B1 + B3, or high-power B8/B28) mix at a bad connector and the resulting odd-order product can land inside your own RX band. That raises the receiver noise floor → desensitization → sensitivity/RSSI degrades even though the transmitter is perfectly clean. It is worst in FDD (TX and RX are on at the same time through a shared antenna/duplexer path).Sources & fixesPIM sourceFixUnder/over-torqued connectorstorque to spec — the #1 field causeDissimilar / ferromagnetic metals (Ni, steel)use silver/tri-metal plating, avoid ferrous parts in the RF pathContamination / corrosion / moistureclean mating surfaces, weatherproofLoose, kinked or damaged cable / braidreplace; ensure solid shield contactMechanical stress / vibration on jointsstrain-relief; the “rusty-bolt effect” is dynamic PIMHow it is measuredDrive two high-power carriers (typically 2×43 dBm / 20 W) into the DUT and measure the IM3 product falling in the RX band. Re-torque, swap jumpers, and re-test before blaming the RFFE. PIM is external and mechanical far more often than it is a chip fault.Interview Q&AQ: How is PIM different from the IP3 / active intermodulation you measure with ACLR?
a: IP3/active IM comes from transistors in the PA/LNA and shows up as spectral regrowth (ACLR/EVM) in the transmit path. PIM comes from passive junctions (connectors, metals, corrosion) mixing high-power carriers, and its damage is that odd-order products fall into your own receive band and desensitize the RX — so a radio can pass every active-linearity test yet fail sensitivity because of one bad connector.

q: Why is PIM more of a problem in FDD than TDD?
a: In FDD the transmitter and receiver operate simultaneously through a shared antenna/duplexer, so PIM products generated by the strong TX carriers are present exactly when the sensitive RX is listening. In TDD the RX listens only when the TX is off, so self-generated PIM cannot fall on the receiver at the same instant.

q: What is the image frequency and which architecture suffers from it?
a: The image is the unwanted frequency located 2×IF away from the wanted signal that mixes down to the same IF, so it cannot be separated after mixing. It afflicts the superheterodyne receiver, which is why an image-reject filter or image-reject mixer is required ahead of the mixer. Zero-IF has no image (IF = 0) but trades it for DC-offset and I/Q problems.

q: Why is direct-conversion so popular in RUs and phones despite DC offset and I/Q imbalance?
a: It removes the image and the bulky IF filtering, needs very few external components, and integrates the whole receiver onto one transceiver chip — cheap, small, low-power and multi-band. Its impairments (DC offset, I/Q imbalance, flicker noise) are correctable in the digital baseband, so the trade is worth it.

q: Why does the loss of the same coax cable increase with frequency?
a: Because of the skin effect: skin depth shrinks as 1/√f, so at higher frequency the current is confined to an ever-thinner surface layer, raising the conductor’s AC resistance and therefore the dB/m loss (roughly ∝ √f). That is why your jumper eats more dB at n41 than at B8 and why loss must be calibrated per band.

q: Why are RF connectors and conductors silver-plated rather than just solid copper?
a: Because RF current flows only in the surface skin depth, the surface conductivity is what matters. Silver has slightly higher conductivity than copper, so a thin silver plating lowers surface resistance and loss for far less cost than a solid silver conductor; it also resists corrosion that would otherwise raise loss and cause PIM.

q: What is the difference between an isolator and a circulator?
a: They are the same ferrite non-reciprocal device; a circulator has 3 (or more) usable ports that pass power in a rotational order (1→2→3→1), while an isolator is a circulator with one port terminated in a matched load, leaving a 2-port device that passes the forward wave and absorbs the reverse. Use a circulator to route TX/RX on one antenna, an isolator to protect a single stage.

q: Why put an isolator after the PA?
a: To protect the PA from reflected power. If the antenna is mismatched (high VSWR), the reflected wave would otherwise re-enter the PA output, causing heating, gain compression, instability or damage. The isolator passes the forward signal to the antenna and diverts the reflected wave into a load.

q: Envelope Tracking and DPD both sit around the PA — what different problems do they solve?
a: DPD solves linearity: it pre-distorts the input to cancel the PA’s AM/AM and AM/PM distortion so ACLR and EVM pass. ET solves efficiency: it modulates the PA’s supply voltage to track the signal envelope so the PA is not wasting DC power at backoff. One keeps the spectrum clean, the other keeps the PA cool and power-efficient; high-end radios use both.

q: Why does a high-PAPR OFDM signal make a PA inefficient?
a: A linear PA sized for the peaks must run several dB below its peak on average (backoff). With a fixed supply, the difference between the supply rail and the low instantaneous envelope is dissipated as heat, so average efficiency collapses. Envelope tracking or Doherty recover that by matching the supply/load to the envelope.

q: Why is self-interference in a full-duplex radio around 100 dB, and why does that make it so hard?
a: Because the transmitter output (order of watts, ~+30 dBm) and the wanted received signal (order of −90 dBm) differ by roughly 100–120 dB, yet they share the same frequency and time, so ordinary frequency/time filtering cannot separate them. You must cancel the TX from the RX by ~110 dB across antenna, analog-RF and digital domains — including modelling PA non-linearities — which is why in-band full-duplex is still largely experimental.

q: How is full-duplex different from FDD, which also transmits and receives at once?
a: FDD does transmit and receive simultaneously but on different frequencies, so a duplexer filter separates them. In-band full-duplex uses one single frequency for both directions at the same time, so there is no frequency (or time) separation to exploit — the radio must actively cancel its own transmission.

q: BLER is 20% at −65 dBm. The sensitivity limit is −68 dBm. What's happening?
a: At −65 dBm (3dB above the limit), BLER should be near 0%. 20% BLER at this power indicates: LNA degraded, cable fault, DSA mismatch, or HARQ is disabled/misconfigured. Check: sensitivity test at −50 dBm first — if BLER still fails, UL path is broken.

q: What is NDI in the MAC header?
a: New Data Indicator — 1-bit toggle. Flips for a new TB. Stays same for HARQ retransmission. The receiver uses NDI to know: 'is this new data (start fresh combine buffer) or a retx (soft combine with previous)?'. Incorrect NDI = UE discards retx, can't combine = BLER jumps.

q: VoLTE voice quality degrades but RTP stream shows no packet loss. What RLC mode is voice?
a: VoLTE voice uses RLC UM mode — no retransmission. Packet loss at RLC level directly becomes voice quality loss. The issue is at L1/L2 (BLER, HARQ), not RLC. Check: PDCP discard timer, HARQ BLER in that sector, and UL power control for the UE.

q: Why does RLC exist if HARQ already handles retransmissions?
a: HARQ is limited to 4 rounds over 8ms — leaves residual BLER ~1%. For best-effort data (file download), 1% BLER over time compounds to significant loss. RLC AM ARQ handles the residual failures. HARQ = fast and hardware; RLC ARQ = reliable and software.

q: Why is integrity protection only for SRBs and not DRBs?
a: Adding 4-byte MAC-I to every user data packet would add significant overhead to high-speed DRBs (e.g., 100Mbps DRB = 50MB/s × 4 bytes = 200KB/s overhead, plus processing load). SRBs carry RRC/NAS signaling which must not be tampered with — the overhead is acceptable. User data integrity is protected at higher layers (TLS/HTTPS).

q: PDCP sequence number wraps around. What happens?
a: 12-bit SN = 4096 values, 18-bit = 262144. The receiver handles wrap-around using a window. For 12-bit: window = 2^11 = 2048. As long as out-of-order doesn't exceed half the window, reassembly works. In 5G NR with 18-bit SN, wrap-around is much rarer.

q: UE is stuck in RRC_CONNECTED but has no data throughput. Protocol layer issue?
a: Check: 1) DRB is established (RRCConnectionReconfiguration with DRB-ToAddMod). 2) Bearer is mapped to correct S1/NG tunnel (eNB-to-SGW/UPF). 3) UE sent RRCConnectionReconfigurationComplete. 4) Check PDCP ciphering mismatch — if UE and eNB use different keys, data silently dropped.

q: What is SRB1 vs SRB2?
a: SRB1 (Signaling Radio Bearer 1): carries RRC messages AND NAS in RRC message container. Created FIRST in RRC setup — needed for all signaling. SRB2: carries NAS messages ONLY, more protected. Created after security activation. You cannot send NAS directly on SRB1 after SRB2 is set up.

q: What is the difference between S1AP and NAS?
a: S1AP (S1 Application Protocol) is between eNB and MME — carries NAS as a transparent container plus S1AP procedures (bearer setup, handover, paging). NAS is end-to-end between UE and MME — eNB doesn't parse NAS, just forwards it. S1AP is per-eNB/per-UE context; NAS is per-UE/per-MME context.

q: UE authentication keeps failing in lab. What do you check?
a: 1. SIM/USIM Ki matches what's programmed in HSS. 2. OPc vs OP — network uses one, SIM configured for other. 3. SQN (Sequence Number) out of sync — HSS SQN too far ahead of USIM counter. 4. Algorithm mismatch — UE supports MILENAGE but HSS using TUAK. 5. Check NAS logs: look for EMM Cause IE in Attach Reject.

q: BLER is 0% at your sensitivity test point. Is this a pass?
a: Check the power level. If BLER=0% AT the sensitivity limit power → PASS (better than spec). If 0% but you haven't decreased to the limit yet → keep decreasing power until BLER hits 5%, that's the actual sensitivity point. Your automated test does a 3-stage search specifically to find this point.

q: What is HARQ process 0 vs process 7?
a: 8 HARQ processes run independently in parallel — like 8 separate ARQ instances. Process number identifies which soft combine buffer to use. Process 0's buffer is separate from process 7's. A TB arriving in subframe N uses the same process ID as its potential retransmission in N+8. If the IDs don't match → UE resets buffer → can't combine → BLER increases.

q: Handover success rate drops to 80%. What do you investigate?
a: 1. Measurement config: A3 offset too large → HO triggers too late (RLF before HO). 2. TTT (Time To Trigger) too long → same issue. 3. X2 interface down → falls back to S1 (slower). 4. Target cell admission control rejecting → load issue. 5. PRACH config mismatch on target → UE can't complete RACH.

q: What is the difference between handover and cell reselection?
a: Cell reselection: UE is in RRC_IDLE. UE autonomously selects best cell based on S/R criteria (RSRP thresholds, hysteresis). No signaling to network. Handover: UE is in RRC_CONNECTED. Network commands the UE to move (UE reports measurements, eNB decides). UE cannot initiate handover — it only executes it.

q: SCell is configured but throughput didn't double. What do you check?
a: 1. SCell activation: MAC CE activation command sent? (check L2 logs for SCellAct). 2. SCell PDCCH: is gNB scheduling on SCell? Check DL grant count per CC. 3. UE capability: UE-CapabilityInformation includes ca-BandCombination? 4. RF: SCell RSRP > threshold for activation? 5. Power: Pmax split correctly between PCell/SCell?

q: VoLTE call drops after 30 seconds. SIP stays up. What's wrong?
a: SIP is the signaling — stays up. RTP is the media — must be flowing. If call drops after 30s: 1) RTCP: no RTCP packets received for 30s → UE/network considers call dead (RTCP timeout). 2) GBR bearer dropped (PCRF withdrew QCI=1 bearer). 3) RTP jitter buffer overflow. Check: eNB bearer logs for QCI=1 DRB status.

q: Why does VoLTE use AMR-WB instead of G.711?
a: AMR-WB (Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband): 50-7000Hz frequency range, 12.65kbps. G.711: 300-3400Hz, 64kbps. AMR-WB gives better voice quality (HD voice) at 5× lower bitrate. Lower bitrate = smaller GBR = fewer radio resources = more VoLTE calls per cell. AMR-WB also adapts codec rate based on radio conditions.

q: Your O-RU fails to connect to DU. You see eCPRI link up but no data. Where do you debug?
a: eCPRI physical layer is up (link up). Likely M-plane (NETCONF) issue: 1) NETCONF connection to DU? Try: netopeer-cli connect to DU IP. 2) O-RU not configured: check if DU sent the o-ran-interface-config. 3) Timing: PTP sync not established? O-RU won't pass C/U-plane without sync. 4) eCPRI C-plane: is DU sending Section descriptors? Check OAM counters.

q: What is the F1 interface used for?
a: F1 connects gNB-CU to gNB-DU. F1AP handles: UE context setup (F1AP: UEContextSetupRequest), RRC message transfer (DLRRCMessageTransfer/ULRRCMessageTransfer), and F1 setup procedure (F1SetupRequest). F1-U is the GTP-U user plane between CU-UP and DU. The split means: RRC/PDCP logic is centralized, MAC/PHY is distributed at the site.

q: EN-DC configured but UE only shows LTE, no NR. What are the steps?
a: 1. Confirm UE is EN-DC capable (UE-CapabilityInformation in logs — look for en-DC-Parameters). 2. NR SCell RSRP > B2 threshold (or A4 event) to trigger SgNB addition. 3. X2 link between eNB and gNB is up? (X2 setup procedure). 4. PLMN and TAC correct on gNB? 5. Bearer type: does policy allow SCG bearer? Check PCRF/MME for SN bearer approval.

q: CMAS alert is not reaching UEs even though CBC says success. What do you check?
a: 1. eNB received Write-Replace Warning Request (S1AP logs). 2. eNB is scheduling SIB12 (check SIB scheduling log). 3. UE is camped on the correct PLMN and TAC. 4. UE emergency alert enabled (device settings + SIM country). 5. SIB12 content: messageId and serialNumber match expected. 6. UE CMAS capability in UE-CapabilityInformation.

q: UE keeps oscillating between two cells every 30 seconds. Root cause?
a: Ping-pong: Q_hyst too small or T_reselection too short. Both cells have similar RSRP → small signal fluctuation causes reselection back and forth. Fix: increase Q_hyst to 4-6dB, increase T_reselection to 4-5s. Also check if the two cells are co-sited (high correlation = real coverage overlap issue requiring tilt/power optimization).

q: You're testing 5G n78 100MHz. SCS=30kHz. How many subcarriers?
a: 100MHz / 30kHz = 3333 subcarriers — but that's not how it works. NR uses resource blocks. 100MHz at 30kHz SCS: from 3GPP 38.104 Table 5.3.2-1, the max RBs for 100MHz @30kHz = 66 RBs × 12 subcarriers = 792 active subcarriers (with guard bands). Carrier actually uses ~98MHz of occupied spectrum.

q: Why does 5G NR support multiple numerologies instead of just one?
a: Flexibility: FR2 mmWave at 28GHz with 120kHz SCS keeps symbol duration at 8.3μs — appropriate for indoor/outdoor mmWave deployment where multipath delay spread is small. FR1 at 700MHz with 15kHz SCS gives 66.7μs symbol + 4.7μs CP — needed for rural macro cells with large delay spread. One-size-fits-all like LTE would be suboptimal.

q: What is SUCI and why does 5G use it instead of sending IMSI in plaintext?
a: SUCI = Subscription Concealed Identifier. The IMSI (SUPI in 5G) is encrypted using the home network's public key before being sent over the air. Even if an attacker captures the Registration Request, they can't read the subscriber identity — only the home network (UDM/SIDF) can decrypt it. LTE sends IMSI in plaintext in the first Attach Request — a known privacy weakness.

q: PDU session established but no IP connectivity. What do you check?
a: 1. UPF GTP-U tunnel: SMF sent PFCP Session Establishment to UPF? 2. gNB GTP endpoint correct in NGAP PDUSessionResourceSetupResponse? 3. DRB established on gNB and UE? 4. IP address assigned (check PDU Session Accept message for UE IP). 5. UPF routing: can UPF route to DN (Data Network)? 6. DNS: UE gets an IP but DNS fails?

q: Intra-CU inter-DU handover fails. F1AP UEContextSetupResponse not received from target DU. Cause?
a: 1. Target DU overloaded (admission control rejection). 2. F1 interface down to tDU. 3. Target cell not configured on tDU (check cell config). 4. ARFCN/PCI mismatch in HandoverRequest vs tDU actual config. 5. F1AP message version mismatch. Check: tDU F1 setup status, cell operational state, F1AP logs on both sides.

q: Your RCT passes all tests. But field team reports low throughput in that sector. What do you investigate?
a: Lab pass ≠ field pass. Check: 1) Cable losses different in field (longer cable runs). 2) Environmental factors (temperature → PA gain drift). 3) Interference from neighbouring operators (not present in lab). 4) Antenna tilt/azimuth (mechanical vs electrical). 5) Backhaul bandwidth bottleneck. 6) UE distribution — lab uses ideal UE, field has real UEs at various distances.

q: What's the difference between pilot pollution and high interference?
a: Pilot pollution: many cells of similar strength — SINR is low because the reference signal from all cells adds as noise to each other. High interference: one or few dominant interferers at specific frequencies. Pilot pollution is a geometry problem (too many equal servers); interference is a frequency/power problem.

q: Place this on the axes: UE moves from B3 cell on eNB-A to B1 cell on eNB-B, both on the same MME, X2 present.
a: Inter-frequency, inter-band, intra-RAT, inter-eNB, X2-based handover. Because the ARFCN changes, the source configures measurement gaps before the A3 report; because there is an X2 link, it is an X2 handover with a final S1 path-switch to the S-GW.

q: Difference between intra-DU, inter-DU and inter-CU handover in 5G?
a: Intra-DU = cell change inside one DU, handled by the DU (no F1 mobility). Inter-DU (intra-CU) = DU changes but the CU-UP stays, so the PDCP/SDAP anchor and the NG-U tunnel to the UPF are unchanged — only F1 is re-pointed (lowest impact, PT17). Inter-CU = the whole logical gNB changes → full Xn or N2 handover with UE-context transfer and a path switch, like inter-eNB in 4G.

q: Which interface makes CSFB possible, and what attach type does the UE need?
a: The SGs interface between the MME and the MSC/VLR carries the CS paging and the location-update signalling. The UE must perform a combined EPS/IMSI attach so it is simultaneously registered in the PS (EPC) and CS (MSC) domains; otherwise the MSC cannot page it via the MME.

q: What triggers SRVCC and which interface carries the PS-to-CS request?
a: A B2 measurement event (serving LTE below threshold-1 while the target UTRAN/GERAN cell is above threshold-2) makes the eNB send S1AP HandoverRequired with an SRVCC indication. The MME then uses the Sv interface to the MSC Server to request the PS-to-CS transfer, while IMS transfers the session (STN-SR) so the far end is unaffected.

q: Why is eSRVCC better than basic SRVCC?
a: eSRVCC anchors the media at the ATCF/ATGW in the visited network, so at handover only the access leg is switched and the end-to-end media path barely changes — cutting the voice interruption from hundreds of ms to tens of ms.

q: Why do most operators launch 5G SA with EPS Fallback instead of VoNR?
a: VoNR needs the whole chain — NR cell voice scheduling, UE support, IMS over NR, and good NR coverage/latency for a GBR flow — to be mature. EPS Fallback reuses the already-proven VoLTE/IMS stack on LTE, so operators guarantee reliable voice on day one and enable VoNR later as coverage and device support catch up.

q: A 5G SA voice call takes ~2 s longer to connect than data. Why?
a: Almost certainly EPS Fallback: setting up the 5QI=1 flow triggers an inter-RAT move (handover or redirect) to LTE before the call completes, adding the RAT-change time. Confirm by checking for an NGAP handover / RRCRelease-with-redirect right after the IMS INVITE.

q: Difference between RRC_IDLE and RRC_INACTIVE, and why did 5G add INACTIVE?
a: In IDLE the RAN has released the UE context, so resuming needs a full RRC setup plus NAS signalling and core paging over the whole tracking area. In INACTIVE the gNB retains the UE context and the NG connection is suspended, so the UE resumes with a lightweight RRCResume (I-RNTI) and RAN paging within the RNA. 5G added it because smartphones send frequent small bursts — INACTIVE gives near-idle battery with millisecond-scale resume, avoiding the signalling storm of constant IDLE↔CONNECTED transitions.
tags: lte 5g rrc protocol call-flow idle-mode mobility

q: A UE reads a SIB before it has a connection — which channels does the SIB travel on, top to bottom?
a: Logical BCCH → transport DL-SCH → physical PDSCH, and the PDSCH carrying that SIB is scheduled by a DCI on PDCCH (SI-RNTI). Only the MIB uses the BCCH→BCH→PBCH path; all other system information (SIBs) rides the shared channel PDSCH.
tags: lte protocol phy channel call-flow fundamentals

q: What is the difference between a control channel and a shared channel?
a: A shared channel (PDSCH/PUSCH) is a common time-frequency resource the scheduler divides among users each TTI and carries the actual transport-block payload. Control channels (PDCCH/PUCCH/PCFICH/PHICH) carry the signalling that makes that scheduling and its feedback work — grants, HARQ ACK/NACK, CSI, SR — not user data.
tags: lte protocol phy channel call-flow fundamentals

q: Why did NR drop PCFICH and PHICH?
a: PCFICH signalled the LTE control-region size (CFI) every subframe — NR instead fixes the control resources via RRC-configured CORESETs, so no per-slot indicator is needed. PHICH gave a 1-bit UL HARQ ACK — NR removed it because asynchronous, DCI-scheduled UL HARQ (with the NDI in the UL grant) is more flexible and supports flexible numerology, so feedback rides normal DCI instead.
tags: 5g nr protocol phy channel call-flow fundamentals ssb

q: Where does SIB1 travel in NR, and how does the UE find it?
a: SIB1 is on the shared channel PDSCH. The MIB (in PBCH within the SSB) points to CORESET#0 / SearchSpace#0; the UE monitors that for a PDCCH scrambled with SI-RNTI, which grants the PDSCH carrying SIB1.
tags: 5g nr protocol phy channel call-flow fundamentals ssb

q: Your DL data decodes fine but the eNB keeps retransmitting — which control channel is involved and what likely failed?
a: The DL HARQ-ACK the UE sends on PUCCH (or piggybacked on PUSCH). If the eNB does not receive the ACK it assumes NACK and retransmits — so the problem is UL PUCCH reliability/coverage or a mis-decoded UCI, not the PDSCH itself. Check PUCCH SINR / format and UL power control.
tags: lte 5g protocol phy channel pdcch pucch dci uci call-flow

q: What is a CORESET and why did NR introduce it?
a: A CORESET (Control Resource Set) is the block of resource blocks and OFDM symbols where PDCCH can be transmitted, configured by RRC. NR uses it (with search spaces) instead of LTE fixed control region + PCFICH, giving flexible, beam-friendly, bandwidth-part-specific control placement.
tags: lte 5g protocol phy channel pdcch pucch dci uci call-flow

q: What is the difference between DL-SCH and PDSCH?
a: DL-SCH is the transport channel — the MAC-layer view (a transport block with HARQ, dynamic MCS). PDSCH is the physical channel — the actual modulated resource elements that carry that transport block over the air. DL-SCH is mapped onto PDSCH.
tags: lte 5g protocol phy channel pdsch pusch tx rx measurements

q: Besides user data, what else travels on PDSCH?
a: SIBs (system information beyond the MIB), paging messages, and RRC signalling (e.g. RRCSetup, reconfiguration) — all ride DL-SCH → PDSCH, because only the MIB uses the separate PBCH path.
tags: lte 5g protocol phy channel pdsch pusch tx rx measurements

q: Contention-based vs contention-free RACH — when is each used?
a: Contention-based is for initial access when the network does not know the UE yet: the UE picks a random preamble, so collisions are possible and are resolved at Msg4. Contention-free uses a preamble the network pre-assigned (e.g. in the handover command), so there is no collision and access is fast/deterministic — used for handover, DL data arrival, and positioning.
tags: lte 5g protocol call-flow phy prach rach initial-access

q: Which RACH message carries the RRCSetupRequest, and what ID does the UE use before it has a C-RNTI?
a: Msg3 on PUSCH carries the RRCSetupRequest. Before contention resolution the UE is addressed via the RA-RNTI (for Msg2/RAR) and a TC-RNTI (temporary C-RNTI granted in the RAR); after Msg4 the TC-RNTI is promoted to the C-RNTI.
tags: lte 5g protocol call-flow phy prach rach initial-access

q: On which interface and protocol does a handover-prep message travel in LTE, vs the user data being forwarded?
a: Handover preparation is X2AP over SCTP on the X2-C interface (eNB-to-eNB); the buffered/forwarded user data during the handover goes over X2-U as GTP-U tunnels. If there is no X2, prep falls back to S1AP over S1-MME via the MME.
tags: lte protocol architecture s1ap x2ap transport

q: Why does 5G add the F1 and E1 interfaces that did not exist in LTE?
a: Because the gNB is disaggregated into CU and DU (and the CU into CU-CP/CU-UP). F1 (F1-C/F1-U) connects the CU to the DU across the midhaul, and E1 connects CU-CP to CU-UP. This split lets operators centralise PDCP/RRC in the CU while keeping RLC/MAC/PHY near the radio in the DU — the basis of O-RAN and cloud-RAN.
tags: 5g nr protocol architecture ngap xnap f1ap oran transport

q: Why page across a whole Tracking Area list instead of the last known cell?
a: An idle UE reselects cells autonomously and does not tell the network each move, so the network only knows the TA-list granularity. Paging the whole list guarantees reachability; the trade-off is paging load vs TAU signalling — a smaller TA list means precise paging but more frequent tracking-area updates.

q: Difference between DRX and eDRX?
a: DRX cycles are short (hundreds of ms to a few seconds) for normal phones balancing latency and battery. eDRX extends the cycle to seconds/minutes/hours for IoT devices that tolerate high latency, drastically cutting power at the cost of reachability delay.

q: What does the UE actually measure and report for beam management, and how does the gNB tell it which beam to receive on?
a: The UE measures L1-RSRP per SSB index (P1) or per CSI-RS resource (P2/P3) and reports the strongest beam(s). The gNB signals the active beam via a TCI state, which QCLs the PDCCH/PDSCH DMRS to a given SSB/CSI-RS so the UE applies the matching Rx beam.
tags: 5g nr protocol phy beamforming mimo measurements

q: LTE uses QCI per bearer — what is the 5G equivalent and what is different?
a: 5G uses 5QI per QoS Flow (QFI), not per bearer. Multiple QoS flows share a PDU session and are mapped to DRBs by the SDAP layer (which LTE lacks), giving finer granularity and features like reflective QoS. The 5QI values largely mirror the old QCI table (5QI 1 = voice, 5 = IMS signalling, 9 = default).

q: What is reflective QoS?
a: A 5G feature where the UE derives the uplink QoS-flow-to-DRB mapping by observing the QFI marking on downlink packets, instead of being explicitly configured — reducing signalling for short-lived flows.

q: What is an S-NSSAI and how does a UE end up using a particular slice?
a: An S-NSSAI (SST + optional SD) identifies a slice. The UE sends a Requested NSSAI at registration; the AMF, with the NSSF, returns an Allowed NSSAI and selects a suitable AMF. When the UE sets up a PDU session it names an S-NSSAI + DNN, and the SMF selects a UPF dedicated to that slice.

q: Why did NR remove the always-on CRS, and what replaced its two jobs?
a: CRS was on all the time regardless of traffic, causing constant interference and power draw. NR removed it for a lean/energy-saving carrier. Its demodulation job is done by on-demand, UE-specific DMRS; its measurement job (RSRP/RSRQ/SINR) is done on the SSB (SS-RSRP) and CSI-RS.
tags: lte 5g nr protocol phy channel measurements

q: On your n41 carrier, what does the field RSRP value come from?
a: NR SS-RSRP — the per-SSB-beam RSRP measured on the SSB (PSS/SSS/PBCH). Because SSB is beam-swept, each beam has its own SS-RSRP, which is also what beam management (BM01) reports.
tags: lte 5g nr protocol phy channel measurements

q: In the AKA procedure, what does AUTN do and why does it matter?
a: AUTN is the authentication token the network sends with RAND; the USIM checks it against its sequence number and MAC to confirm the challenge really came from the genuine home network. That is what makes AKA mutual — the UE authenticates the network, not just the other way around, so a rogue/false base station cannot complete authentication.

q: Where is ciphering actually applied in the LTE/5G stack?
a: On the access stratum it is done in the PDCP layer (RRC signalling on SRBs and user data on DRBs); on the non-access stratum the NAS layer ciphers and integrity-protects its own messages between the UE and the MME/AMF. So a packet can be double-protected: NAS security end-to-core, plus AS security over the radio.

q: What problem does SUCI solve that LTE had?
a: LTE could send the permanent IMSI over the air in the clear (e.g. on first attach or identity request), letting IMSI-catchers track subscribers. 5G encrypts the permanent identity (SUPI) into a SUCI using the home network public key, so only the home network can recover it — closing the identity-privacy hole.

q: What is RSTD and which method uses it?
a: RSTD (Reference Signal Time Difference) is the difference in arrival time at the UE between the PRS of a neighbour cell and a reference cell. OTDOA (DL-TDOA) uses a set of RSTD measurements to place the UE on intersecting hyperbolas. It depends on tight inter-cell synchronisation.

q: Why is multi-RTT more robust than OTDOA?
a: OTDOA relies on cells being precisely time-synchronised, so any inter-cell timing offset becomes a position error. Multi-RTT measures the round-trip time between the UE and each gNB; the round trip cancels the common clock bias, so it tolerates imperfect network sync and typically gives metre-level accuracy.

q: What is ANR and what does it save?
a: Automatic Neighbour Relations: instead of hand-maintaining every cell's neighbour list, the network asks a UE that reports an unknown cell to read its ECGI, then adds the relation and sets up the X2/Xn link automatically. It removes a huge, error-prone manual planning task and keeps neighbour lists correct as the network changes.

q: Explain PCI collision versus PCI confusion.
a: Collision is two adjacent cells using the same PCI, so a UE at their boundary cannot distinguish them (sync/decode fails). Confusion is a single cell having two different neighbours with the same PCI, so a handover request to "that PCI" is ambiguous. Automatic PCI assignment (self-configuration) is designed to prevent both.

q: Why is remote interference a TDD problem and not an FDD problem?
a: In FDD, transmit and receive are on separate frequencies with a duplexer, so a distant cell's downlink can never land in your uplink band. In TDD, all cells use the same frequency and only separate UL/DL by time; if a far cell's downlink is ducted so it arrives during your uplink symbols, it falls exactly on your receive band and time — hence remote interference is unique to TDD.
tags: 5g nr tdd protocol troubleshooting measurements oran

q: What is a RIM-RS and how does it fix the problem?
a: A RIM Reference Signal is a special signal the victim gNB transmits when it detects the sloped remote-interference pattern. Because the propagation duct is reciprocal, the aggressor gNB hundreds of km away detects that RIM-RS, learns it is the source, and applies mitigation — backing off the downlink symbols near the DL→UL switch and enlarging the guard period so its energy no longer reaches the victim's uplink.
tags: 5g nr tdd protocol troubleshooting measurements oran

q: What does the NNSF do in S1-Flex?
a: The NAS Node Selection Function in the eNB decides which MME in the pool a UE's NAS signalling goes to. For a returning UE it uses the GUMMEI in the S-TMSI to route back to the same MME; for a new UE it picks one using the configured weight factors (capacity-based load balancing).

q: GUMMEI vs GUAMI?
a: GUMMEI (LTE) globally identifies an MME (PLMN + MME Group ID + MME Code); GUAMI (5G) globally identifies an AMF (PLMN + AMF Region + AMF Set + AMF Pointer). Both are embedded in the UE's temporary identity (S-TMSI / 5G-S-TMSI) so the RAN can route signalling to the correct pooled core node.

q: How does pooling give redundancy?
a: Because the eNB/gNB is connected to several MMEs/AMFs, losing one doesn't isolate the cell — its UEs re-establish and the NNSF/AMF-selection routes them to a surviving node in the pool. You can also deliberately drain a node (for maintenance) and its UEs migrate to peers.

q: Why does the frame-offset unit matter for TDD alignment?
a: Because the offset is written to the FPGA in samples at 122.88 MS/s (~8.138 ns each); if you assume the YANG-declared 1.2288 GHz unit you are off by 10×, and the DL/UL switch points land in the wrong place — breaking UL reception and, across cells, causing cross-link/remote interference.
tags: 5g nr tdd lte protocol phy measurements

Pass = throughput ≥ 95% at the reference level. RX combining gain — the number people forgetThe 3GPP number above is per single RX port. The product combines multiple RX branches, so the system-level sensitivity is better than the single-port figure by the combining gain:• Mid band (B1/B3): 4-RX combining → ≈ +6 dB• Low band incl. B28: 2-RX combining → ≈ +3 dBSo a single-port measurement of ~−104 to −105 dBm on B28 becomes ~−107 to −108 dBm after 2-RX combining. Always state which one you're quoting — comparing a single-port measurement against a combined requirement (or vice-versa) is the #1 cause of a "sensitivity looks short" false alarm. B28 has less combining headroom (3 dB) than mid-band (6 dB), so it's the first to look marginal. The isolation sequence (run in this order) 1 · Pin the firmware. Record the FHGW FW version the shortfall was seen on, and re-measure on a second FW build — rules out a FW/calibration regression before you touch hardware. 2 · +5 dB ADC attenuation, then re-measure. This is the key discriminator: • sensitivity degrades with +5 dB → not enough system gain / RX gain margin → investigate the RX gain path (LNA, front-end, DSA/ADC_ADJUST). • sensitivity ≈ unchanged with +5 dB → the ADC input level isn't the limiter → look at the DU / UL demod / BLER measurement path (decode, not RF). 3 · Change the test frequency. Move to a different (clean) in-band frequency. If it recovers, you had external RF interference, not an RU fault — verify the frequency is clean first. 4 · Compare to a reference/certification measurement. Line it up against a known-good result, but normalise first: account for the combining gain (2-RX vs single port) and any difference in the cable-loss application method — don't chase an absolute-value gap that's just a measurement convention. How the ADC-attenuation check looks at the CLIget-atten-dfe <ant> <cc> <atten×10> sets the digital front-end ADC attenuation; then inject the FRC and read power-monitor (UL dBFS), get-rssi (dBFS/dBm) and BLER. If adding attenuation barely moves BLER/sensitivity, the limit is downstream (DU/demod), not the ADC input. Interview Q&A Q: A B28 unit looks ~3 dB short on RX sensitivity — how do you debug it?
a: First check it isn't a measurement mismatch: the 3GPP number is per single RX port, but B28 uses 2-RX combining (~3 dB), so confirm I'm comparing like-for-like and normalise the cable-loss method. Then pin the FW version (re-test on a second build), add +5 dB ADC attenuation — if sensitivity degrades it's an RX-gain/system-gain problem (LNA/front-end/DSA), if it's unchanged the limit is in the DU/UL-demod/BLER path — and finally move to a clean frequency to rule out external interference.

q: Why does mid-band have more sensitivity margin than B28?
a: Combining gain. Mid band (B1/B3) combines 4 RX branches (~6 dB), low band including B28 combines only 2 (~3 dB), so B28 has half the combining headroom and shows up marginal first.

q: What does adding ADC attenuation tell you in a sensitivity investigation?
a: It separates an RF-gain limit from a decode limit. If +5 dB of ADC attenuation worsens sensitivity, the RX chain didn't have enough gain margin; if sensitivity barely moves, the ADC input level isn't the bottleneck and the problem is downstream in the DU/UL demodulation/BLER path.

Before this, TX conformance measured the summed signal from all PAs — so if one RFFE/pol was bad you couldn't tell which. Isolation turns off every path but one, so the analyzer sees just that PA. "IQ playback" = the DU replays a pre-generated IQ ETM waveform (deterministic, TX-only) rather than live PHY.How it works (tx_speed.py:771 → rffe.py)_run_iq_playback_measurements, gated on iq_playback=True AND rrh.tx_per_rffe_enabled() (rrh[0].RFFE AND rffe_control.tx_per_rffe).per ETM: connect_cli_manager -> telnet localhost:8888 (root/root, '>' prompt) per IQ port (pol A/B/C/D via iq_playback_ant_map): iq_playback {ETM.bin} {port} 0 0 ; wait 5s ; rrh.rffe_restore_all per RFFE 1..N: rffe_isolate(band,rffe,pol): mb-modify-rffe band-id: B1=1 B3=3 B8=8 B28=9928 B41=41 (TX not stopped) wait settle_sec (7s) rffe_verify_isolated -> mb-get-pa : only target ENABLED else tag ISOLATION_UNCONFIRMED _iq_measure_one -> measure_test_Tx_* (ACLR/EVM) row tagged RFFE{n}{pol}_ant{k} rffe_restore_all (at end and on failure)Modes, layout & the two quirks that make it reliableTwo modes: each-RFFE-on-each-pol (per-RFFE isolation) and all-RFFE-on-each-pol (0xf baseline, all PAs). Layout: B1/B3/B41 = "all" (4 RFFE × 4 pol = 16 paths); B8/B28 = "split" (RFFE1,2 → A,B; RFFE3,4 → C,D). Two ECS fixes make it dependable: rffe_restore_all before every measure (else RFFEs stay off → analyzer reads noise, ACLR ≈ 0 / EVM ≈ 90%) and auto-range before ACLR (else the isolated low-power path reads ACLR near the noise floor — see FC01). Run flag: --iq-playback=true. Code: source/products/rrh/mixins/rffe.py (RffeMixin), wired into FHGW.Interview Q&AQ: A per-RFFE isolated path reads ACLR 51 dBc but the combined output passes 55 — is the PA bad? Probably not — check the analyzer auto-ranged (sa_set_atten_for_min_clipping). An isolated single-PA path is lower power, so without auto-range ACLR sits near the noise floor; with it you get ~54.5–55.6.Q: How do you prove only the target RFFE was transmitting? rffe_verify_isolated reads mb-get-pa — if any non-target PA is still ENABLED the row is tagged ISOLATION_UNCONFIRMED, so a bad isolation can't silently pass. (vru.py) FWK4 Framework — S-Plane verification (PTP/SyncE timing) Framework click to expand + The "S" = Synchronization · features/tech_5g/splane_verification_nr.py · docs SPLANE_AUTOMATION_EXPLANATION.md + knowledge_base/splane_verification.md Plain English — what & whyIn an O-RAN 7.2x split the RU must keep its clock aligned to the network using PTP (IEEE-1588) driven by a Grand Master (GM), backed by GNSS + internal oscillator. Get it wrong → TDD breaks, interference, 3GPP timing fails. Two headline metrics: Frequency Error (Hz / ppb) and Time Alignment Error / TAE (ns). The RU cycles PTP states LOCKED → HOLDOVER → ACQUIRING → LOCKED. Measured by a spectrum analyzer (RF freq/time via EVM table) and a Keysight oscilloscope (physical 1PPS / 10 MHz edge). The three test typesHoldover — deliberately kill the reference (GNSS or PTP) so the RU free-runs on its oscillator, then measure drift. GM is forced to HOLDOVER before measuring so the whole window is genuine holdover. Variants: GNSS-loss, PTP-loss (C3 topology), two-GM redundancy (4 h scope capture).Stability — long capture under PTP LOCKED to build statistics (~10 samples/s) + recovery tests (re-lock after PTP restart / full reboot, e.g. "locked in 145.2s").Temperature monitoring — pre-test that waits for thermal equilibrium first, because oscillators drift with temp (TCXO ~±1 ppm/°C) and would contaminate results. Config & pre-test flowGMConfig caches the GM PTP settings (ptp_instance/ptp_port/gnss_port from setup.json "gm"). Cadence hierarchy Cadence-IDs["SPLANE"] → Group-IDs["TS_DL_SPLANE"] → Test-IDs; group carries PreTest[] + Tests[], dispatched via getattr(). Pre-test sequence: wipe FHGW logs → start PTP-packet tcpdump → temperature stabilize → PTP restart → start TX (aborts if all antennas < −20 dBm). PTP-restart polls fetch_lock_state() every 10 s until HOLDOVER, re-enables in a finally, then check_sync_state("LOCKED", timeout=600). Concrete limits & durationsmaxAbsTE < 1100 ns (3GPP, scope — abort on fail) · dTEh < 200 ns (holdover drift rate) · holdover KPIs freq_tolerance 50 ppb, time_offset 300 ns, max_time_error 1500 ns · non-holdover Freq_Error ±185 Hz, TAE 65 ns (±25), EVM 18.5%. Durations: temp stabilize 30 min (±2 °C), holdover/lock timeout 600 s, stability capture 1000 s, scope capture 4 h @ 200 ns/div. Typical "good": ±100 Hz, ±30 ns. NF1 Noise — Thermal floor kTB = −174 dBm/Hz (the absolute limit) Beginner click to expand▾ PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Thermal noise in one sentence: Any object above −273°C (absolute zero) has electrons randomly moving around — that random movement creates a tiny electrical noise. In your RU, every resistive component (cable, duplexer, LNA input) generates this noise. The LNA then amplifies it along with the wanted signal. This is why you cannot build a perfectly silent receiver. Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Thermal noise (kTB) sets the absolute noise floor. NF1 explains the physics. The full sensitivity formula using kTB + NF + SNR → DSA offset is in the DSA card. → For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Thermal Noise — kTB, Johnson-Nyquist, Noise Voltage Johnson-Nyquist Noise Source: random electron motion in resistor Power: P = kTB watts Voltage: Vn = √(4kTBR) volts Independent of resistance value Present in every resistive element in your RU In Your RX Chain Cable termination: generates kTB noise Duplexer resistive loss: generates noise LNA input resistance: generates noise LNA amplifies all of the above Cannot be eliminated — only minimised by design Key Values kTB at 290K, 1Hz: −174 dBm/Hz +10 MHz BW (+70dB): −104 dBm +System NF 5.75dB: −98.25 dBm +SNR_req −1dB: −99.25 dBm = B1 10MHz QPSK sensitivity RCT bench setup — DU, AAU, instruments, connections decoded Your bench setup — instrument roles: EXM E6640A: Vector Signal Generator. Why thermal noise is unavoidable Thermal noise and the sensitivity floor: Any resistive element above 0 K generates thermal noise. In your RX chain: the cable termination, the duplexer, the LNA input — all generate kTB noise. The LNA then amplifies both the incoming signal and all the noise it sees. You cannot eliminate this noise — you can only minimise the noise added after the signal enters the chain (which is what good LNA design does). This is why cryogenic receivers used in radio astronomy cool the LNA to near 0 K — it is the only way to get below the room-temperature kTB floor. Noise voltage — how it appears on a spectrum analyser: Noise voltage Vn = √(4kTBR). For a 50Ω system at 290K in 1MHz bandwidth: Vn = √(4 × 1.38e-23 × 290 × 1e6 × 50) = 0.895 μV = −107 dBm. On your EXA with preamp ON, this appears as the noise floor — the flat baseline across the span. When you inject a signal that rises above this floor, you can measure it. When the signal drops below it, it is lost in the noise. 📐 Real numbers — how temperature changes thermal noise −40°C T = 233K kTB = −175.6 dBm/Hz 1.6 dB better than 290K +17°C T = 290K (reference) kTB = −174 dBm/Hz 3GPP reference temp +55°C T = 328K kTB = −173.5 dBm/Hz 0.5 dB worse +70°C T = 343K kTB = −173.3 dBm/Hz 0.7 dB worse + PA derates The thermal noise change with temperature is small (LNA NF increases and PA gain decreases — both effects are larger than the thermal noise change itself. NF2 Noise — Figure (NF): SNR degradation, Noise Factor, sensitivity Intermediate click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: NF is the SNR degradation caused by your RX chain. It is the third term in the sensitivity formula after kTB+BW. Your system NF = 5.75 dB built up from the Friis chain — see NCH card. Full sensitivity derivation is in DSA card. → For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Noise Figure — SNR Degradation Through Your RX Chain NF Definition NF (dB) = SNR_in (dB) − SNR_out (dB) = how much SNR the device degrades Perfect device: NF = 0 dB (no degradation) Real cable 2.5dB loss: NF = 2.5 dB Your system: NF = 5.75 dB total (B1) NF in Sensitivity Formula Sens = −174 + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_req NF = 5.75 → Sens shifts 5.75 dB worse Perfect RX (NF=0): sens = −104+(−1) = −105 Real RX (NF=5.75): sens = −99.25 dBm 5.75 dB penalty vs theoretical perfect RX NF as SNR degradation — what it means in practice Noise Factor vs Noise Figure: Noise Factor (F) is the linear ratio: F = SNR_in / SNR_out. Always ≥ 1. A perfect device has F = 1. Noise Figure (NF) = 10·log(F) in dB. A perfect device has NF = 0 dB. Your system NF of 5.75 dB means F = 10^(5.75/10) = 3.76 — your chain degrades SNR by a factor of 3.76 (not 5.75 times — remember dB is logarithmic). The sensitivity formula uses NF in dB because all other terms are already in dB. How NF directly sets your test injection level: EXM injects at sensitivity threshold. Sensitivity = kTB_floor + NF + SNR_req. If your NF increases by 1 dB (e.g. cable gets longer, LNA degrades), sensitivity worsens by 1 dB, and EXM must inject 1 dB more power. If EXM is not recalibrated but NF increased, the test is now 1 dB too easy — you are testing above threshold without knowing it. This is why the DSA table is recalculated whenever hardware changes. NF3 Noise — Friis cascade (why the LNA dominates) Advanced click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Friis cascade formula explains how your 5.75 dB system NF is built from individual component NFs. This NF feeds directly into the sensitivity formula. See DSA card for full chain, NCH card for numerical calculation. → For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Friis Cascade — NF_total = NF1 + (NF2-1)/G1 + (NF3-1)/(G1·G2) + ... Before LNA G1 ≤ 1 (passive loss) Full NF penalty Cable+Dup+BPF = 3.3 dB LNA ★ NF=2 dB · G=+20 dB Dominates system NF Place ASAP in chain G=100 linear After LNA G1=100, divide NF 7dB mixer → 0.07dB Completely negligible Key design rules from Friis: 1. First stage NF dominates — LNA quality is critical 2. Minimise ALL loss before LNA (cable, connectors, filters) 3. High LNA gain shields everything after it from noise 4. Improving post-LNA components gives near-zero benefit Why Friis means you only need to care about the LNA The Friis insight — one worked example: Imagine you have a 7 dB NF mixer after your 20 dB gain LNA. Its Friis contribution is (F_mixer − 1) / G_LNA = (5.012 − 1) / 100 = 0.040 linear = 0.17 dB to system NF. Now replace that mixer with a perfect 0 dB NF mixer. System NF improvement = 0.17 dB. Barely measurable. But reduce cable loss before the LNA by 0.5 dB — system NF improves by exactly 0.5 dB, directly improving sensitivity by 0.5 dB. This is the Friis insight: optimise before the LNA, not after it. In your lab: the pre-LNA components you can actually change: The duplexer and pre-BPF are fixed inside the RFFE — you cannot change them. The LNA is a fixed chip — you cannot swap it. The only pre-LNA component you control in the test setup is the cable from EXM to the RU port. Shorter, lower-loss cable = better system NF in your measurement = better apparent sensitivity. This is why cable quality and measured loss matter, and why the VNA cable loss measurement is step 1 of every sensitivity test setup. NF4 Noise — Passive devices (attenuators, cables, filters add noise) Intermediate click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Passive devices add NF equal to their loss — this directly worsens system NF and therefore sensitivity. Every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA = 0.1 dB worse sensitivity. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. NF of Passive Devices — Golden Rule: NF (dB) = Loss (dB) Every passive device with X dB loss adds exactly X dB to system NF — no exceptions Attenuator 10 dB pad NF = 10 dB Use AFTER LNA only Before LNA = disaster Lab cable 2.5 dB loss NF = 2.5 dB Before LNA = full hit Biggest lab variable Duplexer 0.5 dB loss NF = 0.5 dB Always before LNA Cannot move it BPF Filter 0.3 dB loss NF = 0.3 dB Post-LNA: ÷100 = 0.003 Negligible after LNA Same 10 dB attenuator: Before LNA → +10 dB NF After LNA → +0.1 dB NF LNA gain divides all downstream NF by 100× For TX measurements: always put the 30 dB pad AFTER the coupler output (BOB SMA) — never in the RX path Why passive devices add noise equal to their loss A resistor at room temperature generates thermal noise power = kTB. When a passive component like a cable attenuates a signal by X dB, it absorbs part of the signal power and replaces it with its own thermal noise. The result: the signal level drops by X dB but the noise floor drops by less (because the component adds its own noise). The net effect is exactly X dB of SNR degradation, which is the definition of X dB noise figure. Why position relative to LNA is everything: The Friis formula shows that each stage's NF contribution is divided by the gain of all preceding stages. A component before the LNA (G_preceding = 1 or less) adds its full NF. A component after the LNA (G_preceding = 100 for +20 dB LNA) adds only 1/100th of its NF to the system total. This is why the design rule is: minimise all loss before the LNA, and place the LNA as early in the chain as physically possible. Your duplexer and pre-BPF must be before the LNA for functional reasons (they select the band) but their loss directly degrades sensitivity. Attenuator placement — the most common lab mistake: When measuring TX power with EXA, you add a 30 dB attenuator to protect the EXA from the strong TX signal. This attenuator must go between the RU TX output and the EXA input — never between the signal source and the RU RX input. If you accidentally put the 30 dB pad in the RX path during a sensitivity test, you add 30 dB to system NF, and your measured sensitivity becomes 30 dB worse than reality. Always double-check the signal path before running any RX measurement. Connector loss — the hidden NF contributor: A single SMA connector in good condition has approximately 0.1–0.15 dB insertion loss. That is 0.1–0.15 dB of NF contribution if it is before the LNA. In a chain with 4 connectors before the LNA (source → cable → two adapters → RU port), that is 0.4–0.6 dB of additional NF from connectors alone. A damaged or incorrectly torqued connector can have 0.3–0.5 dB extra loss, immediately visible as sensitivity degradation. This is why the VNA connector inspection checklist exists and why torque specs matter for RF measurements. NF5 Noise — The 5 types (thermal, shot, flicker/1f, white, burst) Advanced click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: 5 noise types exist. Thermal noise (kTB) is what the sensitivity formula is based on. Phase noise limits EVM. Quantisation noise limits ADC dynamic range. All three affect your daily measurements. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. 5 Types of Noise — Sources, Spectrum, Your Lab Impact ① Thermal kTB · Johnson-Nyquist Flat — always present Your main sensitivity floor cause Reduce: narrow BW ② Shot Discrete electrons Flat — in diodes/BJTs In your LNA biasing circuit — small Reduce: lower current ③ Flicker (1/f) Low-freq crystal defects High at low f, flat at RF GaN PA issue <1 MHz Upconverts to LO skirts Reduce: GaAs over Si ④ Phase Noise LO frequency jitter Skirts around carrier Causes EVM floor Limits 64QAM/256QAM Reduce: better VCO/PLL ⑤ Quantisation ADC rounding error Flat — white-like SQNR = 6N+1.76 dB 12-bit → 74 dB Reduce: more ADC bits The three noise types that matter most in your work Of the five noise types, three are directly relevant to your daily testing. Thermal noise sets your sensitivity floor and is the subject of the entire DSA/NF calculation chain. Phase noise from the LO limits EVM and prevents high-order modulations from decoding. Quantisation noise from the ADC sets the dynamic range ceiling. ① Thermal noise — your sensitivity floor: Generated by any resistive element at temperature above 0 K. Formula: P = kTB. In your RX chain, every lossy component (cable, duplexer, filter) generates thermal noise equal to its loss in power. The LNA amplifies both the signal and all the noise it sees, but its own added noise is small (NF = 2 dB). This is the noise the entire DSA framework is designed around — calculate it, characterise it per band, then test each band against its own correctly-adjusted threshold. ④ Phase noise — why it shows up in EVM failures: The local oscillator (LO) that downconverts your RF signal to baseband is not a perfect single frequency — it has random phase jitter. This jitter appears as noise skirts around the carrier in the frequency domain. When the LO mixes with your signal, this phase jitter gets transferred to the baseband IQ constellation — the symbol points rotate slightly randomly, which increases EVM. Phase noise is why you see an EVM floor that does not improve even when SNR is excellent. For QPSK this is not a problem, but for 64QAM and 256QAM the tighter constellation margins make phase noise the limiting factor. ⑤ Quantisation noise — ADC dynamic range: Every ADC rounds the analog signal to the nearest discrete level. With 12 bits, there are 4096 levels. The rounding error is the quantisation noise. SQNR = 6.02 × N + 1.76 = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74 dB. This means your ADC can cleanly handle signals up to 74 dB above the quantisation noise floor. If your signal swings too close to full scale (clipping), you get heavy distortion. If it is too weak (near the quantisation floor), you lose resolution. The VGA/AGC in your RX chain keeps the signal in the sweet spot — typically around −12 dBFS, well within the 74 dB dynamic range.
