NF Applied to Your Work — EXA Preamp, Per-Band Sensitivity Budget EXA N9010B Preamp Settings Setting DANL @ 2 GHz Atten 20 dB, preamp OFF: −103 dBm/Hz ← TX ACLR / power Atten 0 dB, preamp OFF: −120 dBm/Hz Atten 0 dB, preamp ON: −130 dBm/Hz ← RSSI / sensitivity Preamp = internal LNA — adds gain → lowers EXA's own NF NEVER use preamp for TX — overloads input → compression Rule: signal > −30 dBm → preamp OFF · signal < −60 dBm → preamp ON Per-Band Sensitivity Budget (10 MHz) Band NF(dB) Sensitivity DSA B1 2.44 −99.3 dBm 5 dB B3 2.40 −99.4 dBm 0 dB ← baseline B8 3.15 −98.6 dBm 8 dB B28 2.73 −99.0 dBm 8 dB B41 2.00 −99.8 dBm 5 dB (TDD) Sensitivity = −174 + 70 + NF + (−1) for QPSK 1/3 How NF directly drives everything in your daily test work NF is not an abstract concept — it is the single number that determines what power the EXM must inject for each band, what the EXA DANL must be to measure it, and whether a sensitivity failure is a hardware problem or a calibration issue. Every time you set up a sensitivity test, you are implicitly using NF. EXA DANL must be lower than RU sensitivity — always check: DANL (Displayed Average Noise Level) is the EXA's own noise floor — the minimum signal it can measure. For your sensitivity test to be valid, the EXA's DANL must be significantly lower than the signal you are trying to measure at the RU output. In your test: EXM injects at sensitivity threshold (e.g. −97.5 dBm at RU port after cable). The PRACH detector inside the RU processes this. You read the result via CLI (get_rssi) or DU RSSI — you are not measuring the raw RF signal with EXA at this point. The EXA is used for TX measurements. But if you ever try to measure a weak RX signal directly with EXA, the DANL check is critical: EXA DANL at −130 dBm/Hz across 10 MHz = −130 + 70 = −60 dBm — safely below your −98 dBm system noise floor. Why B8 has the highest NF (3.15 dB) and highest DSA: At 900 MHz (B8), the transistor physics in GaAs/GaN LNAs produce slightly higher noise compared to 2 GHz. Additionally, the duplexer for B8 at 900 MHz is physically larger and has higher insertion loss than at 2 GHz — the filter Q-factor degrades at lower frequencies meaning you need a wider physical filter to achieve the same selectivity, which adds loss. These two effects combine to give B8 the worst NF in your band set. B41 at 2545 MHz has the best NF (2.0 dB) because there is no duplexer — TDD uses a T/R switch which has lower loss than a duplexer. When measured sensitivity is worse than calculated — NF-based diagnosis: If your sensitivity test fails by X dB, and you have confirmed cable loss and EXM calibration are correct, the excess degradation must come from the RX chain NF being higher than assumed. Break it down: measure cable loss with VNA → subtract from EXM output → compare to sensitivity formula → if residual error > 1 dB, the RX chain NF is degraded. The most likely causes in order: (1) LNA compression from a too-strong signal on a different port, (2) LNA bias voltage wrong after firmware change, (3) duplexer damaged (cracked ceramic), (4) connector oxidised adding loss before LNA. NF_CAL Noise — NF calibration (Y-factor, ENR, hot/cold) Advanced click to expand▾ PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST NF calibration in one sentence: This is how you measure whether your LNA and RX chain are generating as little noise as expected. You inject two known noise levels (hot and cold) and measure how much noise the chain adds — that added noise is the Noise Figure. It tells you if the hardware is healthy, but it does not write any correction values. Quick link — how this connects to DSA: NF calibration uses the Y-factor method to measure actual system NF. This confirms whether NF matches the values used in the sensitivity formula. It does not write any correction — it only validates hardware health. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. NF Calibration — Y-Factor Method (Hot/Cold Noise Source) Noise Source HOT: ENR=15dB T_hot ≈ 9600 K DUT (your RU) NF = ? dB LNA + duplexer chain EXA measures N_hot = −60 dBm power in measurement BW Noise Source COLD: source OFF T_cold = 290 K DUT (your RU) same gain, same BW EXA measures N_cold = −66 dBm 6 dB lower (Y=4 linear) Y-Factor calculation: Y = N_hot / N_cold (linear) = 10^(6/10) = 3.98 ≈ 4.0 NF = ENR − 10·log(Y−1) = 15 − 10·log(3) = 15 − 4.77 = 10.2 dB ENR = Excess Noise Ratio of source Your RU measured NF targets (at RU input port, after duplexer+cable subtracted): B1: 2.44 dB B3: 2.40 dB B8: 3.15 dB B28: 2.73 dB B41: 2.00 dB What is NF calibration? NF cal answers one question: how much noise does your RX chain add to the signal? This is a hardware characterisation measurement — it tells you whether the LNA, duplexer, and cable are performing to spec. It does NOT write any correction value — it just confirms (or flags) the hardware quality. Key terms, each explained ENR — Excess Noise Ratio The "how much hotter than room temperature is the noise source" spec. ENR=15 dB means the source outputs noise equivalent to a resistor at 290 × 10^(15/10) ≈ 9200 K when switched ON. This is the known reference your calculation depends on. The noise source module has its ENR printed on it and also stored in its EEPROM so the EXA can read it automatically. Y-factor Y = N_hot / N_cold in linear power. If hot output is −60 dBm and cold output is −66 dBm, the difference is 6 dB → Y = 10^(6/10) = 3.98. The Y-factor is how much "more noise" comes out when you switch the source hot vs cold. A low Y means the DUT is adding so much noise of its own that the source temperature barely matters — i.e., high NF device. A high Y means the DUT is quiet and is faithfully amplifying the difference — i.e., low NF device. T_hot and T_cold T_cold = 290 K (standard room temperature, the IEEE reference). T_hot = 290 × 10^(ENR/10). When the noise source is OFF, it still generates thermal noise at 290 K — that becomes your cold reference. This is why you use the same physical source for both measurements: it removes cable and connector uncertainty from the result. NF formula: NF = ENR − 10·log(Y−1) Where this comes from: NF definition is SNR_in/SNR_out. For a two-port device with gain G and noise temperature T_e, the output noise is G·k·(T_cold + T_e)·B for cold input and G·k·(T_hot + T_e)·B for hot input. Taking the ratio cancels G and B, and solving for T_e gives you NF = 10·log(1 + T_e/T_0). Substituting T_e from the Y-factor ratio gives the formula above. In your lab — no standalone noise source needed The EXA N9010B has a built-in NF measurement mode under Meas → Noise Figure. It drives its own internal noise source through Port 1 output, sweeps frequencies, and automatically computes NF vs frequency. You connect EXA Port 1 → RU RX port (via calibrated cable), tell it your cable loss, and it plots NF(f) for you. You then read off the NF at your band centre (e.g. 1950 MHz for B1 UL). The EXA handles the Y-factor math internally. When NF is worse than spec — what to check If measured NF > spec by more than 1 dB: (1) Check cable loss — every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA adds 0.1 dB to measured NF. (2) Check connector torque — loose SMA can add 0.3–0.5 dB. (3) Check LNA bias — wrong supply voltage shifts NF. (4) Check for LNA compression — if signal level too high, LNA is not in its linear region and NF appears worse. (5) Duplexer damage — a damaged duplexer filter adds extra loss before the LNA, directly adding to NF. GAIN_CAL Gain calibration — RX chain ADC_ADJUST, TX power trim, what each register means Advanced click to expand▾ PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Gain calibration in one sentence: This is how you teach the radio to report accurate power readings. You inject a signal of exactly known power, see what the radio reports, and find the offset between them. That offset (ADC_ADJUST) is saved so future readings are accurate. RX gain cal = RSSI cal — they are the same procedure called by two different names. Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Gain cal (= RSSI cal for RX, power trim for TX) corrects the difference between theoretical and actual chain gain. Gain Calibration — RX and TX Chain RX Gain Cal (finds ADC_ADJUST): EXM injects −95.0 dBm known exactly Cable −2.5 dB −97.5 RU RX chain dup+BPF+LNA +VGA+mixer ADC −12.5 dBFS get_rssi reads ADC_ADJUST = ? = P_at_RU_port − dBFS = −97.5 − (−12.5) = −85 dBm/dBFS offset Written to hardware.json: "ADC_ADJUST_B1": −85, "ADC_ADJUST_B3": −84.5, separate per band, per ADC ch TX Gain Cal (trims output power to rated target): BBU sets TX_GAIN reg integer 0-255 DAC→PA RFFE TX chain DPD+CFR active BOB SMA coupler output −16.7 dBm target EXA measures actual: −17.9 dBm error = −1.2 dB Adjust TX_GAIN +1.2 dB → increment register by ~4 counts re-measure → repeat PASS: |error| ≤ 1 dB write final reg value to tx_calibration.json TX rated targets at BOB SMA: B1=−16.7 · B3=−15.7 · B8=−18.0 · B28=−27.3 · B41=−23.0 dBm These are the power levels seen at the coupler output — full antenna power is ~30 dB higher after the coupler ratio RX Gain Calibration — what ADC_ADJUST really is The RX chain has many components between the antenna port and the ADC register: duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer, another BPF, then the ADC. Each one has gain or loss. Rather than calibrating each component separately, RX gain cal treats the entire chain as a black box and finds one single number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any dBFS reading into an accurate dBm reading at the RU input port. ADC_ADJUST A calibration constant stored in hardware.json, one per band per ADC channel. Formula: ADC_ADJUST = P_known_at_RU_port − dBFS_reading. Once calibrated, converting any future reading is: P_dBm = dBFS + ADC_ADJUST. It absorbs the total chain gain between RU port and ADC register — so even though the LNA adds +20 dB, the VGA might be at +6 dB, and the mixer has conversion loss of −7 dB, you never need to know each individual value. The single offset does it all. Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel Each band has a different LNA gain and filter response, so the total chain gain is different per band. B1 at 2140 MHz has slightly different gain than B3 at 1843 MHz — even though they may share physical hardware, the frequency-dependent component behaviour means each band needs its own cal constant. Per ADC channel (B1 uses ADC channels 0/1/4/5, B3 uses 2/3/6/7) further accounts for ADC input impedance variation and any mismatch in the IQ paths. Temperature dependence — why RSSI can drift LNA gain changes with temperature — typically −0.02 to −0.05 dB/°C for GaAs pHEMT LNAs. In a hot lab (40°C vs 25°C calibration temp), the LNA gain drops ~0.3–0.7 dB, which makes RSSI read 0.3–0.7 dB low. If you see systematic RSSI error that grows as the RU warms up, this is why. Some RU designs have temperature compensation tables that auto-correct ADC_ADJUST as a function of measured board temperature — check hardware.json for a TEMP_COMP array. TX Gain Calibration — what TX_GAIN register controls The TX chain starts with the baseband IQ signal at full digital scale, passes through the DPD block, DAC, upconverter, PA driver, and finally the main PA. The total gain from baseband to RF output is roughly fixed by hardware, but there is always ±2–3 dB unit-to-unit variation from component tolerances. TX gain cal trims a digital attenuator (or the PA bias point) until the output power at the coupler port exactly hits the rated target. tx_calibration_eeprom.json This is the file that holds the final TX_GAIN register values after calibration — one per band per column (A/B/C/D). It is written during factory calibration and stored in the RU EEPROM. When the RU boots, it reads this file and loads the register values before enabling TX. If this file is missing or corrupt, the RU falls back to default gain values which can be 6 dB low or high — this is exactly what caused the ~6 dB B41 power deficit you found on unit 26050509 (fault 12: missing tx_calibration_eeprom.json). Coupler ratio — the BOB SMA is not antenna power The BOB SMA port is a directional coupler output, not the main antenna port. The coupler splits a small fraction of the TX power for monitoring — typically the coupling ratio is 30 dB, meaning the BOB SMA sees 30 dB less power than what goes to the antenna. So B1 rated power at BOB SMA = −16.7 dBm corresponds to +13.3 dBm at the antenna connector, or roughly 21 W EIRP per column after antenna gain. Always measure at the BOB SMA — connecting EXA directly to the antenna port would overload it instantly. DPD and its interaction with gain cal DPD (Digital Pre-Distortion) must converge before you measure TX power — it actively adjusts its coefficients for 30–60 seconds after power-on or after any power level change. If you measure output power while DPD is still adapting, you will see power fluctuating ±0.5 dB and possibly a wrong ACLR. Always wait for DPD to converge (check the DPD status register or simply wait 60 s) before taking a TX power or ACLR reading used for gain calibration. Gain cal vs RSSI cal — how they relate They are the same operation from opposite ends of the RX chain. RSSI cal (ADC_ADJUST) calibrates the entire RX path as one unit. NF cal measures just the noise-adding property of that path. TX gain cal calibrates the TX path. All three together ensure that when EXM injects −95 dBm, the RU reports −95 dBm via get_rssi, and when the BBU commands rated TX power, the antenna port outputs exactly rated power. Any mismatch between these three is a sign something has drifted or failed. Sensitivity — Power Levels on One Scale (B1, 10 MHz) kTB floor: −104 dBm (10 MHz) — pure physics, no device +NF 5.75 dB → system noise floor: −98.25 dBm SENSITIVITY: −99.25 dBm — your PRACH test threshold (B1, 10 MHz, QPSK 1/3) At this power: BLER just hits 5%. Below = link fails. Above = link works. kTB at 1 Hz: −174 dBm/Hz — absolute floor, no physics can beat this Sensitivity = −174 + 10·log(BW_Hz) + NF + SNR_required What sensitivity physically means Sensitivity is the minimum signal power at the RU antenna port at which the receiver can still decode data at 5% BLER (3GPP threshold). It is not fixed — it depends on bandwidth, modulation, and band. The sensitivity formula is not an approximation — it is an exact derivation from thermal physics and information theory. Sensitivity vs RSSI — the critical difference: Sensitivity is a threshold — the floor below which decoding fails. RSSI is a measurement — the actual received power at any instant. During a sensitivity test you set EXM to exactly the sensitivity threshold and verify the RU can decode. In normal operation RSSI is whatever arrives — could be −70 dBm (UE nearby) or −105 dBm (UE at cell edge). Sensitivity defines where the floor is. RSSI tells you where you currently are relative to that floor. Why bandwidth degrades sensitivity — the bucket analogy: A wider channel (wider bandwidth) collects more thermal noise — like a wider bucket catches more rain. The signal power stays fixed but noise increases, so SNR worsens and you need a stronger signal to decode. 5 MHz sensitivity is 3 dB better than 10 MHz. 20 MHz is 3 dB worse than 10 MHz. This is why the DSA table has separate rows for each BW — same band, different thresholds. BLER 5% — why this specific threshold: 3GPP defines sensitivity as the point where Block Error Rate = 5%. Below this, too many blocks fail and the system cannot sustain a call. At 5% BLER the link is just barely functional — this is the edge of coverage. The test is binary: inject at threshold power, count block errors, pass if BLER ≤ 5%. This is measured via the PRACH detection rate in your RCT — PRACH preamble either detected or not. This card explains what drives it: modulation order and coding rate. QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest) sensitivity — this is why FRC A1 is the standard sensitivity test. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Modulation Order vs Required SNR — Why QPSK = Best Sensitivity QPSK 1/3 4 points · 2 bits/sym SNR = −1 dB Best sensitivity FRC A1 — sensitivity test B1: −99.25 dBm Points far apart = robust 16QAM 1/2 16 points · 4 bits/sym SNR = +12 dB 13 dB worse than QPSK FRC A3 B1: −86.25 dBm Points closer = more SNR 64QAM 1/2 64 points · 6 bits/sym SNR = +18 dB 19 dB worse than QPSK FRC A5 B1: −80.25 dBm Points very close = fragile Coding rate — protection vs efficiency: Rate 1/3: 1 data bit → 3 bits sent (2/3 redundancy) Rate 1/2: 1 data bit → 2 bits sent (1/2 redundancy) Rate 3/4: 1 data bit → 1.3 bits sent (little redundancy) Lower rate = more protection = lower SNR needed = better sens Higher rate = more data = higher SNR needed = worse sensitivity Sensitivity test always uses QPSK 1/3 (FRC A1) — max protection High MCS (64QAM 3/4) used for peak throughput tests, not sensitivity What is FRC and why it determines sensitivity FRC (Fixed Reference Channel) is a 3GPP-defined test waveform with fixed modulation, coding rate, and resource allocation. Different FRCs test different capabilities. FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) tests sensitivity because it gives the most robust link — maximum coverage, minimum signal requirement. The sensitivity number you compare against in your DSA table is always FRC A1. Why QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest dBm) sensitivity: QPSK has only 4 constellation points — they are spread far apart in the IQ plane. Even with heavy noise, the receiver can correctly decide which of the 4 quadrants the received symbol falls in. The 1/3 coding rate adds heavy redundancy — for every bit of data, 2 extra error-correction bits are sent. Together these give an effective SNR requirement of −1 dB, meaning the signal can be 1 dB below the thermal noise floor and still be decoded. This is why QPSK 1/3 gives the best sensitivity and is the standard for coverage-limited testing. It solves the problem of testing multiple bands with one test framework: each band has a different sensitivity because each band's hardware (LNA, duplexer, filter) has different noise figures. Rather than hardcoding different thresholds manually, DSA calculates a per-band offset from the sensitivity formula and instructs EXM to inject exactly the right power for each band automatically. Step 1 — kTB: the physics floor kTB = Boltzmann constant × Temperature × Bandwidth. At room temperature (290 K), in a 1 Hz bandwidth: kTB = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm/Hz. This is the absolute minimum noise any receiver can have — it cannot be beaten. For your 10 MHz channel: add 10·log(10,000,000) = +70 dB → noise floor = −104 dBm. For 5 MHz: +67 dB → −107 dBm. For 20 MHz: +73 dB → −101 dBm. Every 2× increase in bandwidth raises the noise floor by 3 dB. Step 2 — System NF: what your hardware adds Noise Figure is how many dB of extra noise your RX chain adds on top of kTB. Your chain (B1): cable 2.5 dB + duplexer 0.5 dB + pre-BPF 0.3 dB + LNA 2.0 dB + post-LNA components ≈0 dB = 5.75 dB system NF. The Friis formula shows that LNA dominates because everything after it gets divided by LNA's linear gain (×100). Everything before the LNA (cable, duplexer, BPF) adds its full loss as NF — this is why cable length matters enormously for sensitivity. Per-band NF: B1=2.44 dB · B3=2.40 dB · B8=3.15 dB · B28=2.73 dB · B41=2.00 dB. B8 highest because 900 MHz LNA has higher noise, and the B8 duplexer has more loss at lower frequency. B41 lowest because TDD uses a T/R switch instead of a duplexer — less loss before the LNA. Step 3 — Sensitivity: combining it all Sensitivity = kTB_floor + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_required SNR_required depends on modulation and coding rate. For FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) — the standard sensitivity test — SNR_req = −1 dB. QPSK has only 4 constellation points spread far apart, so the receiver can decode it even when signal is 1 dB below the noise floor. B1 worked example: −174 + 70 + 5.75 + (−1) = −99.25 dBm B3 baseline: −174 + 70 + 5.71 + (−1) = −99.29 dBm (slightly better NF) B8 worst: −174 + 70 + 6.46 + (−1) = −98.54 dBm (higher NF = worse sensitivity) Step 4 — DSA offset: per-band correction B3 is the reference baseline (DSA = 0). For every other band: DSA = Sensitivity_band − Sensitivity_B3. This gives the number of extra dB EXM must inject for that band to hit the correct threshold. The DSA values in your table (5 for B1, 8 for B8/B28) also include empirical corrections for path configuration differences (LB uses 2 RX paths vs HB 4 paths), flavour-specific gain settings, and actual measured hardware performance — not just the theoretical NF difference alone. Step 5 — RX paths: what rev5/rev1/comb mean Your AAU is 4T4R — 4 independent RX columns (A, B, C, D), each with its own LNA, cable, and ADC channel. rev5 = Column A tested alone (single path, worst case for that column) rev1 = Column B tested alone (independent verification of second chain) comb rev3 = Columns A+B+C combined via MRC (Maximum Ratio Combining). MRC weights each chain by its SNR and sums them. Gain ≈ +3 to 4 dB over single path. comb rev1 = All 4 columns A+B+C+D via MRC. Best possible. Gain ≈ +5 to 6 dB. Why test single paths? Because MRC hides individual column failures. If Column C's LNA is dead, comb rev1 might still pass — A, B, D compensate. The rev5/rev1 single-path tests catch dead columns that combined results would mask. This is exactly what happened with AAU #510 — B1C and B1D showed dead in single-path but combined was degraded not zero. Step 6 — before vs after: the 0.2–0.5 dB gap explained In the DSA table, every measurement has a "before" and "after" value. The DSA offset is already applied before this comparison — these are NOT showing the DSA offset itself. before = theoretical sensitivity from the formula (what physics says it should be) after = sensitivity measured on real hardware after DSA correction The 0.2–0.5 dB gap = hardware residual: connector insertion loss variation (±0.1 dB), LNA NF not exactly at datasheet (±0.1 dB), filter passband ripple (±0.05 dB), cable slightly different from assumed (±0.1 dB). A healthy unit shows consistent 0.2–0.5 dB residual across all paths. A gap suddenly becoming 2–3 dB on one path = hardware fault on that specific column. This is how you catch degraded LNAs and bad connectors at the measurement level without disconnecting anything. 📐 DSA Worked Calculation — B8 vs B3 reference (step by step) Step 1: Compute sensitivity per band Base: kTB = −174 dBm/Hz BW(10MHz) = +70 dB → floor = −104 dBm B3: NF=2.40 → sens = −104 + 2.40 − 1 = −102.6 dBm B8: NF=3.15 → sens = −104 + 3.15 − 1 = −101.85 dBm B1: NF=5.75 → sens = −104 + 5.75 − 1 = −99.25 dBm B28: NF=3.70 → sens = −104 + 3.70 − 1 = −101.3 dBm B41: NF=2.75 → sens = −104 + 2.75 − 1 = −102.25 dBm Step 2: Compute DSA offset (vs B3 reference) DSA = Sens_band − Sens_B3 (reference) DSA_B3 = −102.6 − (−102.6) = 0 dB (reference) DSA_B8 = −101.85 − (−102.6) = +0.75 dB DSA_B1 = −99.25 − (−102.6) = +3.35 dB DSA_B28 = −101.3 − (−102.6) = +1.3 dB DSA_B41 = −102.25 − (−102.6) = +0.35 dB Positive DSA = inject more power (band is less sensitive) Step 3: How EXM uses DSA Base injection = −95 dBm (arbitrary reference). EXM actual = Base + DSA offset. B3: EXM = −95 + 0 = −95 dBm · B1: EXM = −95 + 3.35 = −91.65 dBm · B8: EXM = −95 + 0.75 = −94.25 dBm After cable loss (−2.5 dB): power at RU port = EXM − 2.5 dB B1 at RU port: −91.65 − 2.5 = −94.15 dBm → compare to sensitivity −99.25 dBm → 5.1 dB above → PRACH detects reliably What the DSA physically is (GRDEV-8102)DSA = the RFDC ADC digital step attenuator on the AAU's RX path — it sits inside the RFSoC, right in front of each ADC, and is set in the personality file rfdc.txt as an opcode-2 entry per tile/block (per ADC channel). Before GRDEV-8102 every band ran DSA = 0 dB.Why it exists: the problem is ADC over-range at the top of the RX range, not sensitivity at the bottom. At DSA=0 the ADC clipped under strong uplink and raised fault id 20 ("RX out of order" / Alarm 20); the DSA backs the signal off ADC full-scale so it stops clipping. It's almost free because the noise floor is set by the LNA at the front (Friis — first stage dominates), not by the attenuator later in the chain — so headroom at the top costs ≤ ~1 dB at the bottom. RSSI Calibration — Manual Steps, Automated via RuAuto, Pass Criterion Manual procedure (one band, one channel): EXM inject −95 dBm known get_rssi 0 read dBFS e.g. −12.5 Compute offset P_port − dBFS −97.5−(−12.5)=−85 Write hw.json ADC_ADJUST_B1 = −85 Flash to RU verify: |CLI−EXM| ≤ 1 dB ✓ Pass criterion: |CLI − EXM| ≤ 2 dB |CLI − DU| ≤ 2 dB Automated via RuAuto (rssi_cal test case in tc_cadence.json): 1. EXM sweeps −60 → −110 dBm in 5 dB steps across all B1/B3/B8/B28/B41 centre frequencies 2. At each step: read get_rssi per ADC channel + DU RSSI from testmac, compute error = EXM − cable − reading 3. Max error per band > ±2 dB → flag RSSI_CAL_FAIL → auto-update ADC_ADJUST → reflash → re-verify Separate ADC_ADJUST per band/column: B1 uses ADC ch 0,1,4,5 · B3 uses 2,3,6,7 · LB (B8/B28) uses separate ADC channels What RSSI calibration actually is RSSI calibration and RX gain calibration are the same procedure with different names. The goal is to find the single offset number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any raw dBFS reading from the ADC into an accurate dBm power level at the RU antenna port. Once calibrated, P_dBm = dBFS_reading + ADC_ADJUST for any signal in that band. The three numbers that must agree within 2 dB: EXM output − cable loss = what arrives at the RU port (your reference, measured physically) CLI get_rssi + ADC_ADJUST = what the RU's ADC chain reports (your calibrated reading) DU testmac RSSI = what the baseband processing chain reports after FFT (another independent path) All three must agree within ±2 dB. If EXM says −97.5 dBm, CLI should report −97.5 ± 2 dBm, and DU should also report −97.5 ± 2 dBm. If CLI is accurate but DU is off, the problem is in the FHGW/baseband path. If both CLI and DU are off from EXM, the ADC_ADJUST value is wrong. Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel: B1 UL (1950 MHz) and B3 UL (1747 MHz) use different LNA gain settings, different filter responses, and different ADC input stages. Even if two ADC channels share the same physical ADC chip, the analog input path leading to each channel varies. Unit-to-unit component tolerance means the ADC_ADJUST for B1 on ADC channel 0 of unit 26050509 will differ slightly from the same channel on unit 26050508. This is precisely what RSSI cal measures and corrects — it is a per-unit, per-band, per-channel characterisation. Common RSSI cal failures and root causes: CLI reads 3 dB low → ADC_ADJUST was set with a different cable. Cable got swapped. Measure new cable loss with VNA and re-run cal. CLI accurate but DU off by 2 dB → FHGW BFP decompression issue or testmac RSSI averaging window mismatch. Check FHGW firmware version. RSSI drifts as unit warms up → LNA gain is temperature-sensitive. Re-run cal at operating temperature (after 30 min warm-up), or check if temperature compensation table (TEMP_COMP in hardware.json) is configured. All bands off by same amount → EXM output power was wrong during cal. Re-verify EXM output with EXA before running cal. ADC channel mapping — which channel reads which band/column: B1 Column A → ADC channel 0 · B1 Column B → ADC channel 1 B1 Column C → ADC channel 4 · B1 Column D → ADC channel 5 B3 Column A → ADC channel 2 · B3 Column B → ADC channel 3 B3 Column C → ADC channel 6 · B3 Column D → ADC channel 7 B8/B28 use 2 RX paths (columns A and B only) → channels 0 and 1 with band-specific ADC_ADJUST values So get_rssi 0 reads B1 Column A. get_rssi 2 reads B3 Column A. This mapping is why if Column C shows a bad RSSI reading (channel 4 for B1), you know exactly which physical LNA and cable path to inspect. must doA UE with no uplink timing sends a random-access preamble; the base station must detect it and reply with a timing advance. Two error rates define the test (RCT clause 8.4): missed detection and false alarm. This is the algorithm behind the FC10 PRACH sensitivity test.Preamble = CP + Zadoff-Chu + guard — baseband generationBase sequence build: DFT → IDFT + frequency shift + CP addition → power scaling (ramp-up) → half-bin shift → configurable frequency shift (from SIB2, in units of 15 kHz subcarriers, with a resampling factor K). Bin distance is 1.25 kHz for formats 0–3.Zadoff-Chu, roots & cyclic shiftsThe signature is a Zadoff-Chu sequence — constant amplitude, one sharp autocorrelation peak, low cross-correlation. The cell broadcasts a root; the 64 signatures (preamble index 0–63) come from choosing a root u and a cyclic shift v. Shift granularity is set by Ncs, which defines the Zero-Correlation Zone (ZCZ).The Ncs / ZCZ / K / roots tradeSettingK (preambles/root)RootsEffectZCZ = 1641small allowable delay, no inter-root noiseZCZ = 12~6/7~10larger allowable delay, higher inter-root noiseAllowable delay per UE = Ncs × FFT_size / 839. Bigger cells need more allowable delay (more cyclic-shift room) → more roots → more inter-root noise. That is the core PRACH planning trade.The FlexRAN-style detectorfront endremove CP → FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers× conjugate of the root ZC (correlation)IFFT → power-delay profiledecisionNoise_est = mean(noise vector)detected if peak / Noise_est > peak-multiplierpeak position → timing advanceThe peak multiplier is the tunable threshold separating a real preamble peak from noise.In RuAutotest_Rx_PRACH plays a PRACH IQ waveform and sweeps the input power down (binary or stepped “sensitivity” search) to find the detection threshold against PRACH_KPI — your PRACH ALGO deck made executable. (See FC10 / FC08T for the trace.)Interview Q&AQ: What do the noise estimator and peak multiplier decide, and what does the peak position give you?
a: The noise estimator computes Noise_est = mean of the noise vector from the post-IFFT correlation; the peak multiplier is the threshold — a correlation peak counts as a detected preamble only if peak/Noise_est exceeds it. The position of that peak in the power-delay profile gives the timing advance sent back to the UE.

q: ZCZ=1 vs ZCZ=12 — which gives more roots and more inter-root noise, and why would you use it?
a: ZCZ=12 gives ~10 roots (K≈6–7 preambles each) and higher inter-root noise, but it also allows a larger allowable delay (Ncs×FFT/839), which bigger cells need so a distant UE’s delayed preamble still lands in its zero-correlation zone. ZCZ=1 packs all 64 preambles on one root with no inter-root noise but only a tiny allowable delay — fine for small cells.

q: Why does a fixed drain voltage waste power at low traffic, and what is the fix?
a: With OFDM the PA must be backed off to handle high PAPR, and at low occupancy it sits deep in back-off where drain efficiency is poor — yet a fixed Vdd keeps burning full drain power. Dynamic Vdd lowers the drain voltage as RB occupancy falls (e.g. B1/B3: 40→32→25 V), moving the efficiency peak to the real operating point.

q: When traffic drops, do you lower Vdd before or after the occupancy change, and why?
a: After. If you lowered Vdd before the load actually dropped, the still-high signal could be pushed into clipping and violate ACLR/EVM. Conversely, when load rises you raise Vdd first. And after any Vdd change you re-tune the CFR working point and DAC current so the radiated power and spectrum stay in spec.

q: Why does an embedded, on-target RCT matter versus the normal DU-based test?
a: It removes the DU and the external test PC entirely — you SSH into the RU and run one command, so you can validate the uplink receiver chain in the factory or field with no test rig, and the results track the DU-based sensitivity to within ~1 dB. That makes it fast, portable and automatable (Python-parseable summary).
tags: rct rx automation lte 5g measurements features framework

q: Why pre-reserve 768 MB of hugepages on a 2 GB box?
a: The PHY decoder needs a large, contiguous, non-swapping memory region; pre-reserving 384×2 MB hugepages guarantees it up front with zero runtime allocation jitter, which keeps the per-step timing deterministic on a memory-constrained (2 GB) FHGW.
tags: rct rx automation lte 5g measurements features framework

q: Why cross-check the RU against a 3rd-party PHY?
a: To prove the sensitivity/BLER numbers come from the actual received signal and standard PHY processing, not a quirk of your own decoder or test harness. Feeding identical FRC/ETM/PRACH waveforms through an independent PHY and matching the results validates both the RU hardware and your RCT chain.
tags: rct rx tx measurements lte automation features

q: Why is the QPSK (A1-3) sensitivity so much better than 64QAM (A5-x)?
a: QPSK carries 2 bits/symbol and tolerates a low SINR, so it decodes at a much lower received power (~−104 dBm); 64QAM carries 6 bits/symbol and needs a far higher SINR, so its sensitivity floor is ~−80 dBm. The ~24 dB gap is the modulation-order vs required-SNR trade.
tags: rct rx tx measurements lte automation features

q: Which clause defines EVM, and which defines reference sensitivity, in LTE 36.141?
a: EVM is clause 6.5.2 (transmitted signal quality, TX side); reference sensitivity is clause 7.2 (receiver characteristics, RX side). They live in different top-level clauses because 6 is transmitter and 7 is receiver.
tags: rct measurements tx rx lte reference standards protocol

q: Why is PRACH not in clause 7 with the other receiver tests?
a: Because clause 7 covers RF receiver characteristics (sensitivity, blocking, selectivity, intermod), whereas PRACH detection is a demodulation/performance requirement — it is in clause 8 (8.4). It tests whether the PHY can detect a preamble at a given SNR/level, not a raw RF receiver property.
tags: rct measurements tx rx lte reference standards protocol

q: What is the difference between BS type 1-C and 1-H in 38.141-1?
a: 1-C is a purely conducted radio tested at its antenna connector. 1-H (hybrid) has an array of transceiver-array-boundary (TAB) connectors: some requirements are verified conducted per TAB connector, while others (e.g. certain emissions/steering) are verified OTA. Fully integrated AAS with no connector are type 1-O and tested under 38.141-2.
tags: rct measurements tx rx 5g nr reference standards protocol

q: Why does an AAU use 38.141-2 (OTA) instead of 38.141-1 (conducted)?
a: A fully integrated active antenna system has no accessible antenna connector — the array and radio are one unit — so power, emissions and sensitivity can only be defined and measured over the air (radiated), in a test range/anechoic chamber. That is the type 1-O / 38.141-2 regime, which also adds beam-direction-dependent requirements (radiated transmit power, spatial emission) that have no conducted meaning.
tags: rct measurements tx rx 5g nr oran reference standards protocol

q: OTA defines both 7.2 OTA sensitivity and 7.3 OTA reference sensitivity level — what is the distinction?
a: OTA sensitivity (7.2) is the declared best-case sensitivity in the most sensitive direction/beam (OSDD-based), while OTA reference sensitivity level (7.3) is the minimum-level conformance figure analogous to the conducted reference sensitivity. Conducted specs only have the reference-sensitivity notion; OTA splits the “how good can it be” from the “minimum it must meet.”
tags: rct measurements tx rx 5g nr oran reference standards protocol

q: What is the difference between a "sanity" and a "road_trip" test in the suite?
a: sanity is a fast smoke test that confirms the setup and a couple of key measurements work before you commit to a long run; road_trip is the full sequential execution of every conformance test in that file — the complete conformance pass that CI runs end-to-end.
tags: rct automation lte tx rx measurements framework features

q: Why does test_Tx_modulation_analysis map to several clauses at once?
a: It is a composite measurement: from one captured waveform the analyzer derives BS output power (6.2), frequency error (6.5.1), EVM (6.5.2) and DL RS power (6.5.4) plus the time offset — so one test efficiently covers what would otherwise be four separate captures.
tags: rct automation lte tx rx measurements framework features

q: What is the difference between the conformance and non-conformance suites?
a: Conformance suites verify the 3GPP TS 36.141/38.141 pass/fail requirements exactly. Non-conformance suites are PW-internal engineering tests that go beyond (or aside from) the spec — e.g. PA/PB power-sharing, PHY profiling, gain characterization, PUCCH and timing-advance test cases, and counter checks — used for debug and characterization, not certification.
tags: rct automation 5g nr lte tx rx measurements framework features

q: What does the _2CC set in conformance_nr_tdd_tx.py verify?
a: The 2-component-carrier (carrier-aggregation) variants: it repeats modulation analysis, dynamic range, TAE, OBW, ACLR and reference sensitivity with two carriers active, to confirm the radio still meets spec when aggregating — the inter-carrier effects (e.g. cross-modulation into the adjacent channel) that a single-carrier run cannot catch.
tags: rct automation 5g nr lte tx rx measurements framework features

q: Where does PA Protection live and why is it not a test of its own?
a: It is a helper module, pa_protection.py, not a test_ function — it is invoked from test_main_procedure. PA protection (~3 dB back-off on carrier activation, adjusting DAC current via rfdc-app) is a safety behaviour applied during bring-up of every run, so it is shared infrastructure rather than a standalone conformance test.
tags: rct automation framework features tx rx protocol reference

q: The e2e location-update flow mentions auth + ciphering — where is that defined?
a: That ties to the security stack (SEC01): the location-update procedure runs AKA authentication and then NAS/AS ciphering + integrity before the UE is served. The e2e test exercises that whole call flow end to end, including the MME overload-reject path.
tags: rct automation framework features tx rx protocol reference

q: What are the three NB-IoT deployment modes and how does the suite pick one?
a: In-band (NB-IoT inside an LTE PRB), guard-band (in the LTE channel guard-band — GBAN), and standalone (its own spectrum — SAL). The suite has one entry point per mode (lte_only / nbiot combined-GBAN / standalone-SAL); the setup's nbiot_test_mode field enables the matching entry and skips the others.
tags: rct automation lte nb-iot tx measurements features

q: Why is NB-IoT ACLR specified at ±300/±500 kHz with a 180 kHz filter instead of the LTE offsets?
a: Because NB-IoT is a 200 kHz carrier, not a 1.4–20 MHz LTE channel, so its adjacent-channel offsets and integration bandwidth are scaled to its own carrier (per TS 36.141 Table 6.6.2.1-2b): ±300 kHz at 40 dB and ±500 kHz at 50 dB, integrated over 180 kHz.
tags: rct automation lte nb-iot tx measurements features

q: What is the difference between LOCKED and HOLDOVER, and why does the test force holdover?
a: LOCKED means the RU is actively synchronised to the PTP grandmaster; HOLDOVER means it has lost the grandmaster and is coasting on its own oscillator, which must stay within a timing/frequency mask for a specified period. The test disables the grandmaster on purpose to confirm the RU enters holdover, holds accuracy, and then re-locks when PTP returns — i.e. it survives a real grandmaster outage.
tags: rct automation 5g nr timing protocol features lab

q: Why capture PTP traffic with tcpdump during the test?
a: To record the actual PTP protocol exchange (Sync/Follow-Up/Delay-Req etc.) into a PCAP so timing anomalies can be analysed offline in Wireshark — correlating a sync failure or holdover entry with what happened on the wire, rather than only seeing the RU's reported state.
tags: rct automation 5g nr timing protocol features lab

q: When would you use binary search vs the sensitivity loop for PRACH?
a: Binary search is fast (~5–7 iterations, ±0.5 dB) — good for CI smoke and quick validation. The 3-resolution sensitivity loop (coarse 2 dB → fine 0.5 → finest 0.1) is slower (~15–25 iterations) but hits ±0.1 dB precision and mirrors the other uplink sensitivity tests, so it is used for final conformance/certification.
tags: prach rx rct measurements features automation

q: What is the difference between miss detection and false alarm in the PRACH result?
a: Miss detection is the percentage of transmitted preambles the receiver failed to detect (the sensitivity metric — must stay ≤1% at the KPI power). False alarm is the probability the detector reports a preamble when none was sent — measured with no signal present. A good PRACH detector keeps both low; the sensitivity search targets 1% miss detection.
tags: prach rx rct measurements features automation

q: Why must all four TRX transmit at full power during the 2G sensitivity test?
a: TS 51.021 §7.3.2 requires the BTS to be in its worst-case realistic operating state — all carriers active at full downlink power in every timeslot — so the receiver is tested with the maximum self-generated interference/desense present, not in an artificially quiet configuration.
tags: rct rx 2g measurements features automation reference

q: What does "static" reference sensitivity mean?
a: It is measured under static propagation — no multipath fading and no frequency offset applied to the wanted signal — so it isolates the raw receiver sensitivity floor. Multipath/fading and TU/RA channel conditions are covered by the separate reference-performance (fading) tests, not §7.3.
tags: rct rx 2g measurements features automation reference

q: To isolate one RFFE for a per-front-end ACLR measurement, which CLI command do you use and which must you avoid?
a: Use mb-modify-rffe, which disables a specific (RFFE, polarisation) PA so only the target front end transmits. Avoid mb-modify-pa — on this hardware it is a per-polarisation broadcast that disables that pol on all four RFFEs at once, so it cannot isolate a single RFFE. set-rffe-switch-state is also non-functional here.
tags: rct tx hardware rffe measurements features aau

q: Why is B28 addressed as 9928 in the RFFE CLI?
a: 9928 is a sentinel control-band id the firmware accepts for B28 — the natural ids 28 and 20 are both rejected. Using 9928 returns real per-RFFE data with the same split-RFFE-per-pol-pair layout as band 8.
tags: rct tx hardware rffe measurements features aau

q: What is the difference between --test-mode conformance and non_conformance?
a: conformance runs the 3GPP TS 36.141/38.141 pass/fail suites; non_conformance runs the PW-internal engineering tests (PA/PB, PHY profiling, gain, PUCCH/TA, counters) that go beyond the spec — see RCT02. The flag selects which suite the same runner executes.

q: What does --cadence control?
a: It selects a named preset from the test-config JSON (P0 full/nightly, P1 smoke, and feature-specific ones) that decides which tests and which band/BW/freq/ETM iterations run — so you scale the same suite from a quick smoke to a full conformance pass without editing code.

q: Why is the ACLR limit relaxed from 55 to 52 dBc on a dual-band run?
a: When two bands transmit together, inter-band cross-modulation products land in each other's adjacent channel — a physical hardware effect, not a DPD/linearity failure. The band_min_limit override (52 dBc for the second-run/dual-band keys) accounts for it so a healthy radio is not failed for a known coupling effect.
tags: rct measurements tx reference features kpi

q: What is the precedence when resolving a KPI threshold?
a: tc_cadence.json RRH-Thresholds override → the KPI JSON (with its frequency/band/BW/ETM-specific entry, e.g. band_min_limit keyed by {fhgw_band}_{dualband_step}) → the hard-coded fallback. The most specific matching entry wins.
tags: rct measurements tx reference features kpi

q: Why is the port power the reference and not the ADC value?
a: The port power is trustworthy because the cable loss and port are already calibrated, so you know it exactly. The ADC value has passed through the whole RX chain (RFFE summing, LNA, filters, ADC conversion) whose gain/offset isn't precisely known per unit — that is exactly what RSSI calibration is measuring and correcting.
tags: rssi rx rct measurements features hardware

q: In Z = X + Y, what is X and where does it come from?
a: X is the total RX-chain gain from the antenna port up to the ADC (band-dependent) — it is read from the gain budget (e.g. 32.75 dB for B1). Y is the swept port input power; their sum Z is the value the ADC/RSSI should report, which is compared against the actual reading to derive the per-ADC offset.
tags: rssi rx rct measurements features hardware

q: Open design question from the walkthrough?
a: Whether to calibrate the real ADC chain (so the raw ADC value is true) or to make the CLI RSSI match the DU-reported RSSI (measured after the FFT) — to be confirmed. This is the CLI-get_rssi vs DU comparison in Module 14.
tags: rssi rx rct measurements features hardware

q: Why is rssi_model_offsets 0 during a characterisation run?
a: Because you are measuring the raw error to derive the correction. If the offset were already applied, get-rssi would read corrected values and error = CLI − EIRP would come out ~0 — you'd be measuring your own correction, not the hardware bias. So you characterise with offset = 0, compute offset = −error, then store it.
tags: rssi rx rct measurements features hardware

q: How is this different from the FC15 ADC_ADJUST offset?
a: ADC_ADJUST is a per-ADC hardware calibration in hardware.json that corrects the dBFS→dBm conversion at the converter. rssi_model_offsets is a higher-level per-model/band/antenna bias in the setup config, added to the final reported RSSI. This characterisation isolates whatever residual bias remains after the DSA/ADC calibration (note B3 already read ~0 because the DSA fixed it).
tags: rssi rx rct measurements features hardware

q: Why can't IQ playback be used to validate uSleep?
a: Because the uSleep detector taps the frequency-domain stream just after decompression (dl_chain_din), whereas IQ playback injects its samples five stages downstream at the WOLA output. The detector therefore never sees the played-back content, so a played waveform can never trigger (or fail to trigger) sleep — the validation must use real DU-generated downlink.
tags: rct tx hardware efficiency features 5g lte

q: uSleep vs Dynamic Vdd — how do they differ and combine?
a: uSleep switches the PA enable off during all-zero OFDM symbols (symbol-rate gating); Dynamic Vdd lowers the PA drain voltage as traffic falls (slow supply modulation). One saves on empty symbols, the other saves on low average load — they are orthogonal and their savings are expected to add.
tags: rct tx hardware efficiency features 5g lte

q: What does the Reboot Cause subsystem give you as a validation engineer?
a: A recorded reason for every RU reboot (watchdog, crash, commanded, power, thermal, etc.). In a 100+ reboot stability run that turns "it rebooted" into a classified, countable signal, so you can separate expected restarts from real faults and hand developers a precise RCA instead of a log dump.

q: What is the BKC and why does it exist?
a: The Best Known Configuration is the release's qualified, known-good image set (per RAT) that has passed RCT and E2E, published with its test scenarios and open issues. It exists so every team runs the same proven build — no "works on my image" — and so regressions are measured against a fixed baseline.

q: Which automation branch do you point a CI run at?
a: The RCT integ/CI branch, which is stabilised roughly daily for CI suites; Develop moves too fast (several updates a day) for a repeatable CI baseline, and E2E integ/CICD is for the end-to-end suite.

q: Why not just use per-carrier digital gain and leave DAC current fixed?
a: Because a high fixed DAC current wastes power and raises the noise floor for every carrier on that DAC. When no carrier needs the top 3 dB of headroom you can lower the shared DAC current (coarse, efficient) and skip digital attenuation entirely; you only fall back to per-carrier digital gain when one carrier genuinely needs the headroom.
tags: tx hardware efficiency rct measurements features

q: Why burn a dummy calibration instead of waiting for the real one?
a: A brand-new board has an empty cal EEPROM and won't transmit safely/correctly without one. The dummy, B41-aligned defaults let you power the unit up and run bring-up/integration immediately; you then schedule a real RF calibration run to replace them, because temperature compensation is only accurate with real measured values.
tags: lab hardware tx rct measurements features

q: Why attenuate the PA more when the unit is cold?
a: Cold silicon has different gain/behaviour, so the design applies extra midboard attenuation while the PAs dissipate heat and bring the unit to its stable operating temperature, then removes it as temperature recovers — keeping output power and spectrum in spec throughout warmup rather than overdriving a cold PA.

q: What is the difference in action between TEMP_HIGH and TEMP_CRITICAL?
a: TEMP_HIGH is a Minor alarm that backs the transmitter off by 1 dB (DAC attenuation) to shed heat while staying on air. TEMP_CRITICAL is a Critical alarm — the unit is dangerously overheating — so it is marked out of order and reboots to protect the hardware.

q: Why read the PMU RESET_REASON register at boot instead of trusting the software log?
a: Because many reboots never reach the software logger — kernel panics, hardware-watchdog trips, brown-outs and bootloader faults. The Zynq PMU latches the hardware reset reason in a register (0xFF5E0220) that survives the reboot, so reading it at boot recovers exactly the causes that would otherwise all masquerade as POWER_ON.

q: What makes a 2CC measurement "composite" rather than just two single-carrier tests?
a: All offsets (ACLR, SEM/OBUE, spurious) are referenced to the outer edge of the whole BS RF bandwidth, not each carrier — so the emission mask and adjacent-channel measurements treat both carriers as one aggregated signal. That catches inter-carrier effects (and, for non-contiguous configs, in-gap CACLR/blocking) that two independent single-carrier runs would miss.
tags: ca lte tx measurements rct feature-testing features

q: What is the difference between the PCell and an SCell in CA?
a: The PCell is the primary cell — it terminates RRC/NAS signalling, carries PUCCH and the security context, and is never deactivated while connected. SCells are secondary carriers added purely for extra throughput; they can be activated/deactivated quickly (MAC CE) and only the PCell handles mobility.
tags: lte-feature lte ca carrier aggregation measurements

q: Why does adding cells strain the fronthaul?
a: Each cell needs its own IQ sample stream to the radio. More cells and wider bandwidth multiply the eCPRI/CPRI data rate and the timing/sync budget, so fronthaul capacity and latency, not just baseband MIPS, often set the cell-count limit.

q: TM3 vs TM4 — when do you use each?
a: TM4 (closed-loop) uses PMI feedback and gives the best throughput when the channel is stable and SNR is high. TM3 (open-loop spatial multiplexing) drops PMI and cycles precoders, which is more robust at higher UE speed where feedback goes stale.

q: What inputs does an LTE scheduler use to allocate resources?
a: Channel quality (CQI/rank), buffer occupancy (BSR for UL), QoS class (QCI/priority/GBR), HARQ state, and a fairness policy. It balances throughput (favour good-channel UEs) against fairness and latency guarantees for GBR bearers.

q: What is HARQ and why does TDD need ACK bundling?
a: HARQ = fast physical-layer retransmission with soft-combining, so a retransmission adds energy rather than replacing the packet. In TDD there are fewer UL subframes than DL, so one UL subframe must acknowledge multiple DL subframes — bundling ANDs those ACK/NACKs (or multiplexes them) to fit the feedback.

q: What does the CFI control and why make it dynamic?
a: CFI sets how many leading OFDM symbols form the PDCCH control region. Fixing it high wastes symbols at low load; fixing it low starves control at high load. Dynamic CFI adapts per subframe so you spend control symbols only when there are DCIs to send.

q: What problem does connected-mode DRX solve, and its key timers?
a: It cuts UE power by letting it stop monitoring PDCCH between bursts. Key parameters: on-duration timer, inactivity timer (extends wake after data), short/long DRX cycle, and the HARQ RTT/retransmission timers. Aggressive DRX saves battery but adds scheduling latency.

q: How do you balance load between an overloaded cell and an idle neighbour?
a: Idle mode: adjust cell-reselection priorities/offsets in SIBs so new camps favour the lightly loaded carrier. Connected mode: use load-based (MLB) handovers/redirection when PRB or connected-user utilisation exceeds a threshold, moving suitable UEs to the neighbour.

q: What is ARP and how does admission control use it?
a: ARP = Allocation and Retention Priority: a priority level plus pre-emption capability and vulnerability. Under congestion the eNB admits higher-priority bearers and may drop/pre-empt lower-priority, pre-emptable ones — so emergency and VoLTE survive while best-effort is squeezed.

q: X2 vs S1 handover — what is the difference?
a: X2 handover goes directly between eNBs with direct data forwarding, so it is faster and lighter on the core — used when an X2 link exists. S1 handover is routed through the MME (and S-GW relocation may occur); it is the fallback when there is no X2 or across MME/vendor boundaries.

q: What do too-early and too-late handover counters tell you?
a: Too-late = the UE hit radio-link failure before handing over — raise sensitivity / lower thresholds or TTT. Too-early = it handed over then immediately failed or bounced back — the trigger fired too soon, so add hysteresis/offset. Wrong-cell = it recovered on a different cell, pointing at a neighbour-list/target selection problem.

q: Why is data forwarding needed at handover and how are duplicates avoided?
a: Without it, packets buffered at the source when the UE leaves would be lost. The source forwards outstanding PDCP SDUs/PDUs to the target; PDCP sequence numbering and status reporting let the target resume in order and discard duplicates, giving lossless (or near-lossless) handover.

q: What happens on radio-link failure — drop or recover?
a: The UE declares RLF after T310 expiry, then attempts RRC re-establishment on a suitable cell. If the target has (or retrieves) the stored UE context, the connection and bearers are restored quickly; if not, it falls back to a full RRC setup / re-attach.

q: What is CSFB and where does RIM help?
a: CSFB moves a UE from LTE to 2G/3G to place a circuit-switched voice call, since EPS is packet-only. RIM lets the eNB pre-fetch the target 2G/3G system information, so the fallback redirection is faster because the UE doesn't have to read all the target SIBs on arrival.

q: Why does the eNB query UE capability, and what breaks if it's wrong?
a: It must know the UE's supported bands, CA combinations, category and features to configure SCells/MIMO/modulation legally. If capability is misread or cached stale, the eNB may configure an unsupported combo (RRC failure) or under-configure (lost throughput).

q: Which QCIs does VoLTE use and why SPS?
a: QCI 5 (non-GBR) for IMS/SIP signalling and QCI 1 (GBR, conversational voice) for the RTP media. SPS pre-allocates the small, periodic voice grants so you avoid a PDCCH assignment every 20 ms — cutting control overhead and boosting the number of simultaneous VoLTE users.

q: Handover vs redirection vs reselection between 4G and 5G — differences?
a: Reselection is idle-mode, UE-driven by SIB priorities. Handover is connected-mode, network-controlled and near-seamless with context/bearer transfer between MME and AMF. Redirection is connected-mode but cheaper — the network releases the UE with a target frequency/RAT and the UE reselects there, trading a short interruption for less signalling.

q: MORAN vs MOCN?
a: Both share the RAN. MORAN gives each operator its own dedicated carrier on the shared radio; MOCN shares the same carrier among operators (multiple PLMNs broadcast on one cell). MORAN is simpler to isolate per-operator; MOCN is more spectrum-efficient.

q: What must come up before an NR cell can serve a UE?
a: Timing/sync and fronthaul, then PHY (SSB burst, numerology, TDD pattern), the F1 setup between CU and DU, and NG setup to the AMF. The UE then finds the cell via SSB, reads MIB/SIB1, and can start random access.

q: Where are the reselection parameters in NR vs LTE?
a: NR: SIB2 (reselection common), SIB3 (intra-frequency), SIB4 (inter-frequency). LTE: SIB3 (serving/intra), SIB4 (intra neighbours), SIB5 (inter-frequency). Mixing the two numbering schemes is a classic interview trap.

q: How does a cell turn a reported PCI into a handover target?
a: Via the Neighbour Relation Table: the PCI from the measurement report is looked up to its CGI and the Xn/X2 peer that serves it. PCIs are reused across the network, so the NRT (populated manually or by ANR reading the target's CGI) disambiguates and gives the transport to send the HO request.

q: What problem does ANR solve?
a: Manual neighbour planning is error-prone and misses relations, causing too-late/wrong-cell handovers. ANR uses UE CGI reporting to auto-add neighbours it discovers and remove unused ones, keeping the NRT correct as the network changes.

q: Xn vs N2 handover in 5G?
a: Xn is the direct gNB-to-gNB path with direct forwarding, analogous to LTE X2 — low latency. N2/NG handover is via the AMF (with possible UPF relocation), used when there is no Xn or across AMF boundaries — analogous to LTE S1 handover.

q: How is Xn different from X2?
a: Functionally similar (direct RAN-node link for mobility and data forwarding) but Xn connects gNBs in 5GS and carries 5G constructs — NG-RAN node IDs, NR cell identities, PDU-session/QoS-flow info — whereas X2 connects eNBs in EPS with E-RAB/bearer semantics.

q: Walk the 4-step RACH procedure.
a: Msg1: UE sends a random-access preamble on PRACH. Msg2: gNB sends the Random Access Response with a timing-advance and UL grant. Msg3: UE sends its RRC connection/setup request on the granted resource. Msg4: gNB sends contention resolution confirming the UE. (2-step RACH collapses Msg1+3 and Msg2+4.)

q: Why are there multiple PUCCH formats?
a: They trade payload vs coverage vs latency. Short formats (F0/F2) give low-latency feedback for small UCI; long formats (F1/F3/F4) spread over more symbols for more bits or better cell-edge coverage. The scheduler chooses per the UCI size and the UE's link budget.

q: What is DCI and why does size alignment matter?
a: DCI is the PDCCH scheduling grant telling the UE where/how its data is (RB allocation, MCS, HARQ, etc.). The UE blind-decodes candidates, so 3GPP caps the number of different DCI sizes it must try — size alignment pads/aligns formats to stay within that budget and keep decoding feasible.

q: MU-MIMO vs SU-MIMO?
a: SU-MIMO sends multiple layers to one UE. MU-MIMO sends layers to different UEs on the same resources, separated spatially by beamforming. MU multiplies capacity when UEs are spatially separable and CSI is good, but needs careful user grouping to limit inter-user interference.

q: How does massive MIMO improve both coverage and capacity?
a: Coherently combining many antennas forms a high-gain, narrow beam steered at the UE — that array gain extends coverage. Because beams are spatially separated, the cell can serve many UEs simultaneously (MU-MIMO), multiplying capacity. Both depend on accurate CSI from SRS/CSI-RS.

q: Why does NR sweep SSB beams?
a: On mid/high band the gNB uses narrow beams, so a single fixed broadcast beam would leave gaps. Sweeping several SSB beams across the sector lets a UE at any angle detect the cell, measure per-beam quality, and report the best SSB — the basis for initial access and beam management.

q: What is CSI-RS used for?
a: It lets the UE measure the DL channel and feed back CSI — CQI (quality → MCS), PMI (precoder), RI (rank), and beam indicators. The gNB uses that to choose modulation, precoding and beams. It also supports beam management and fine time/frequency tracking.

q: Why is SRS so important in TDD massive MIMO?
a: TDD uses the same frequency up and down, so by reciprocity the gNB can infer the DL channel from the UL SRS it measures directly — giving full-dimension CSI for beamforming without relying on limited PMI feedback. Good SRS coverage/scheduling is therefore key to MU-MIMO gains.

q: How does link adaptation choose MCS?
a: It maps the reported CQI (and adjusts with an outer loop from HARQ ACK/NACK) to an MCS that hits a target first-transmission BLER (~10%). If retransmissions rise, the outer loop backs off MCS; if the channel improves, it climbs — maximizing throughput at controlled error.

q: What conditions are needed to use 256QAM on the uplink?
a: High SINR and a clean, linear UE transmit path (low EVM), because dense constellations are error-sensitive. Both UE and gNB must support the 256QAM MCS table, and link adaptation only selects it near-cell where the error target can still be met.

q: How would you tune DRX differently for URLLC vs eMBB background traffic?
a: URLLC needs short (or effectively no) DRX cycles and a long inactivity timer so latency stays low, at a power cost. Background/eMBB traffic can use long DRX cycles and short on-durations to maximise sleep, accepting higher scheduling latency.

q: How does an idle UE receive a page without draining its battery?
a: It only wakes at its own paging occasions, computed from its identity and the paging DRX cycle, and monitors PDCCH for the paging RNTI then. The AMF pages the registration area; on a match the UE runs a service request to move to connected.

q: How does 5G QoS differ from LTE bearers?
a: LTE is bearer-centric (EPS bearer = QCI). 5G is flow-centric: the SMF marks packets with a 5QI per QoS flow, and SDAP maps flows onto DRBs. This is finer-grained — many flows can share or split across DRBs within one PDU session, with the scheduler honouring each 5QI.

q: What is EPS fallback and when is it used?
a: When a UE in 5G SA tries an IMS voice call but the cell/network doesn't support VoNR (or QoS can't be met), the network moves the UE to LTE (handover or redirection) and the call proceeds as VoLTE. It's the interim voice solution until VoNR is deployed.

q: VoNR vs EPS fallback?
a: VoNR keeps the voice call natively on 5G NR (IMS over 5QI 1), giving lower latency and no interruption — but it requires mature NR coverage and QoS. EPS fallback punts the call to LTE/VoLTE when VoNR can't be guaranteed. Operators start with fallback and migrate to VoNR as coverage matures.

q: Why is timing advance needed and what bounds cell size?
a: UEs are at different distances, so without TA their uplinks would arrive misaligned and smear across symbols. The gNB commands each UE's TA so signals land within the cyclic prefix. The maximum TA range (and CP length) bounds the achievable cell radius.

q: What are NETCONF and YANG, and which O-RAN interface use them?
a: YANG is the data-model language describing a node's config/state; NETCONF is the protocol (over SSH) to get/edit that config and receive notifications. In O-RAN they realise the O1 interface between the SMO/EMS and the CU/DU (and the M-plane to the O-RU) for FCAPS.

q: What does NG-Flex (AMF pooling) give you?
a: A many-to-many gNB↔AMF connection so UE signalling is distributed across an AMF pool by weight, and if one AMF fails its UEs can be served by others. It's the 5G analogue of LTE S1-Flex (MME pooling) — load balancing plus geo-redundancy.

q: How accurate is E-CID and when would you use it?
a: It's coarse (tens to hundreds of metres) because it leans on cell ID, TA and signal-strength/angle measurements rather than dedicated positioning signals. You use it as a low-cost, always-available baseline, escalating to OTDOA/multi-RTT/PRS when you need higher accuracy.

q: What is NSA / EN-DC and why did operators start there?
a: NSA (EN-DC) attaches a 5G NR secondary node to an existing LTE anchor and EPC, so the LTE cell handles mobility/signalling while NR boosts throughput. It let operators launch 5G data without first deploying a 5G core — faster and cheaper than standalone.
tags: nr-nsa 5g nr lte endc architecture protocol

q: Walk the SgNB addition in EN-DC.
a: The UE sends a B1 measurement report (NR above threshold) to the MeNB. MeNB → SgNB Addition Request (X2AP) with UE capabilities/QoS. SgNB admits, allocates NR resources, replies with its RRC config. MeNB relays it to the UE (RRC reconfiguration). UE performs random access to the gNB and sends reconfiguration complete → the NR leg is active.
tags: nr-nsa 5g nr lte endc call-flow protocol

q: Why gate EN-DC/SCell addition on measurements?
a: Adding an NR leg or SCell that the UE can't sustain wastes signalling and can hurt throughput/battery. Triggering on measurement events (e.g. B1 for NR) ensures the extra carrier is added only when the UE genuinely sees usable quality, and dropped when it fades.

q: What are the EN-DC bearer types and what does split bearer do?
a: MCG bearer uses only the LTE leg, SCG bearer only the NR leg, and split bearer uses both — a single PDCP entity distributes PDUs over the LTE and NR RLC paths and reorders at the receiver. Split bearer aggregates throughput but needs PDCP reordering to handle the two legs' different delays.

q: When is data forwarding needed in NSA?
a: On SgNB change or release (and at split-bearer reconfiguration), packets buffered on the NR leg would otherwise be lost. The source forwards outstanding PDCP PDUs to the new node or the master over X2-U, and PDCP sequencing preserves order and removes duplicates.
tags: nr-nsa 5g nr lte endc handover protocol

q: What limits how many carriers a UE can run across LTE CA + EN-DC?
a: The UE's supported band combinations and its baseband/RF and power budget. Each added carrier costs processing and (for UL) transmit power; the UE advertises the legal combinations in its capability, and the network must stay within them.

q: How is voice handled in NSA?
a: As VoLTE on the LTE anchor — NSA has no 5G core, so voice uses the existing EPC/IMS path (QCI 1). The NR secondary node only adds data throughput; the network may release the NR leg if it threatens the voice bearer's quality or the UE's power budget.
tags: nr-nsa 5g nr lte endc call-flow volte

q: How does NR-leg mobility work in NSA without dropping the connection?
a: The LTE MeNB stays the anchor; only the secondary node changes via SgNB change (add target, release source) triggered by NR measurements, with PDCP data forwarding. Because control/mobility is anchored on LTE, the 5G leg can be swapped underneath without a full handover.

q: Why run NSA and SA on the same NR cell?
a: It lets operators migrate gradually: legacy EN-DC handsets keep working via the LTE anchor while newer SA-capable devices use the 5G core on the same carrier — no separate NR deployment per mode. The gNB must terminate both X2 (to the eNB/EPC) and NG (to the 5GC).

q: What role does X2 play in EN-DC?
a: It connects the MeNB (LTE) and the en-gNB (NR). X2-C carries the SgNB addition/modification/release and coordination signalling; X2-U carries user-plane data forwarding for SCG/split bearers. It's the backbone that makes dual connectivity work.
tags: nr-nsa 5g nr lte endc protocol architecture

q: How do you validate an RU's transmit power?
a: Drive the RU to a known configured power, measure the actual output on a calibrated analyser per antenna/carrier, subtract the measured cable/setup loss, and check it lands within tolerance of target. Deviations point to PA gain, calibration, or a bad TX branch.
tags: common-feature rct tx aau rffe measurements

q: How should a radio handle a recoverable fault?
a: Detect and classify it by fault ID, attempt the least-disruptive recovery first (re-init the affected function), and record the cause and action for root-cause analysis. Only escalate to a full reboot if targeted recovery fails — minimizing outage and giving traceability.

q: What are the O-RAN fronthaul planes and what does M-plane do?
a: C-plane (scheduling/beamforming commands), U-plane (IQ user data), S-plane (timing/sync), and M-plane (management). M-plane uses NETCONF/YANG to configure, software-manage and monitor the O-RU; aggregation lets a manager front many O-RUs' M-plane to the SMO.

q: How do you make a field firmware upgrade safe?
a: Verify the image (signature/checksum), write to an inactive bank so the running one is untouched, activate with a controlled reboot, and auto-roll-back to the previous bank if the new image fails health checks. A/B banking means a bad upgrade never bricks the radio.

q: Why have a heartbeat between OAM and the radio?
a: To detect loss of management connectivity quickly and deterministically — a few missed heartbeats flag the node down and kick off alarms/recovery, catching silent link or process failures that wouldn't otherwise surface until a user-impacting fault.

q: What is GTP-U and why count it?
a: GTP-U is the user-plane tunnelling protocol carrying subscriber data across S1-U/F1-U/N3, keyed by TEIDs per bearer/flow. Per-tunnel counters (packets, bytes, dropped, error indications) let you localise packet loss and throughput bottlenecks to the transport rather than the air interface.

q: What is the E2 interface and the near-RT RIC for?
a: E2 links RAN nodes to the near-real-time RIC, letting xApps subscribe to metrics (KPM service model) and issue control (RC service model) on a ~10 ms–1 s loop — e.g. traffic steering or interference control. A unified E2-plane exposes different RAT nodes to the RIC the same way.

q: What is fronthaul split 7.2x and why was it chosen?
a: It splits the PHY so the O-RU handles low-PHY (iFFT/CP add, digital beamforming) and the O-DU handles high-PHY and above, exchanging frequency-domain IQ over eCPRI. Compared with a full-PHY-in-radio (option 8/CPRI) it cuts fronthaul bandwidth while keeping the radio relatively simple — the O-RAN mainstream choice.

q: What are the benefits and challenges of 4G+5G on one BBU?
a: Benefits: less hardware/power/space, shared transport and timing, and easy EN-DC anchoring. Challenges: partitioning CPU/accelerator and fronthaul capacity so neither RAT starves the other, and keeping timing/sync and software lifecycles for both stacks isolated yet coordinated.

q: Why integrate external/environmental alarms with RAN OAM?
a: So site conditions (power loss, high temperature, intrusion) surface in the same fault management as radio alarms, letting operators correlate and act before an environmental problem forces a thermal shutdown or outage — rather than discovering it only after service drops.

q: Why is timing/phase sync so critical in TDD, and how is it delivered?
a: In TDD all cells must switch between UL and DL at the same instant; a phase error means one cell transmits while a neighbour is receiving, causing cross-link interference. Sync is delivered by GNSS and/or PTP (1588) with SyncE over the fronthaul (the O-RAN S-plane), holding phase within tens of nanoseconds.

q: AAU powers on but the fronthaul (FH) LED is "amber"-ish (green fast blink)? This AAU uses green/red only — a green fast blink on FH LED 1 = PTP Holdover (fault 17): the link is up but the RU has lost lock to the grandmaster and is coasting on its internal clock. Check the PTP grandmaster / timing source and the fronthaul path. (A green slow blink instead = still trying DHCP — no IP yet, check the DHCP server / FH VLAN.)Q: The FH/PTP LED is red — what does that affect? Solid red = fronthaul link down; red slow blink = PTP-sync unlocked/freerun; red fast blink = DHCP failure (fault 18/26). Losing PTP means the RU has no valid network timing → TDD frame alignment and S-plane sync break, so carriers won't come up correctly and RCT can't run. Fix timing/fronthaul before anything else.
