q: When would you reach for QXDM over Wireshark?
a: Wireshark shows the network side (S1/NG, GTP, core). QXDM shows what the UE actually saw and did — the RRC/NAS it decoded, its L1 measurements, its HARQ/BLER and scheduling. For a UE-specific failure (bad HO, wrong measurement report, chipset quirk) QXDM/QCAT is the definitive view.

q: How do you drive many UEs at once with ADB?
a: Each device has a unique serial; address it with adb -s . A script iterates serials to start data, launch iperf/dialer, read modem state, and reboot in parallel — the basis of multi-UE orchestration (UE03).

q: Why orchestrate multiple UEs instead of one?
a: A single UE can't load a cell or expose scheduler fairness, capacity limits, or multi-user interference. Running a fleet in parallel reproduces real cell load, aggregate throughput, and mobility churn — the conditions where most field defects appear.

q: Robot Framework vs pytest — when each?
a: pytest is code-first and great for engineers writing rich Python logic (the RCT conformance suites). Robot is keyword-driven and reads almost like English, so it suits large mixed-skill test teams and reusable keyword libraries for UE/system regression. Both can call the same device/instrument libraries.

q: TM500 vs a commercial UE?
a: TM500 gives deterministic, scriptable, high-count load for base-station capacity/throughput/mobility testing. A commercial UE gives real chipset behaviour (IMS/VoLTE quirks, band-combo support) for interoperability. You use TM500 for scale/repeatability and real UEs for realism (UE08).

q: Where does Amarisoft fit in a validation lab?
a: It provides a controllable reference network or reference UE. Point a real UE at the Amarisoft cell to isolate UE behaviour, or run Amarisoft UE-sim against your gNB to isolate the base station — a cheap, scriptable way to bisect where a problem lives.

q: What does a drive test add over lab RCT?
a: Lab RCT proves the radio meets spec in controlled conditions; a drive test proves coverage, mobility and KPIs in the real RF environment — multipath, interference, real UE distribution — which the lab cannot fully reproduce.

q: Why validate with commercial UEs if you have a TM500?
a: Because operators' subscribers use commercial phones. Only real chipsets reveal IMS/VoLTE behaviour, band-combo negotiation, and vendor-specific interpretations of 3GPP that a deterministic emulator will not — which is exactly what breaks in the field.

q: Why measure both TCP and UDP throughput?
a: UDP at a forced rate reveals the true PHY/MAC capacity and packet loss; TCP reveals what a real application achieves after congestion control and RTT. If UDP is high but TCP is low, the radio is fine and the problem is latency/loss/buffering.

q: Why run 72-hour and reboot-loop tests if the feature already passes functionally?
a: Functional tests catch logic bugs; endurance/stress catch time-and-repetition bugs — memory leaks, handle exhaustion, clock/sync drift, and one-in-hundreds race conditions on reboot. Those are exactly the failures that take down a live network, so they must be found before release.

q: Conformance vs interoperability — why both?
a: Two vendors can each pass conformance yet still fail together because the spec allows options or is read differently. Conformance proves spec compliance in isolation; interoperability proves the RAN, core and real UEs actually interwork — which is what the operator ultimately buys.

q: list vs tuple vs set vs dict — when do you use each?
a: list = ordered, mutable sequence (a sweep of results); tuple = immutable record (a fixed (band, freq) pair, usable as a dict key); set = unique membership with O(1) lookups (which preambles were detected); dict = key→value mapping (per-band limits, per-ADC offsets). Pick by whether you need order, mutability, uniqueness, or lookup.

q: Why use 'with open(...)' instead of open()/close()?
a: The context manager guarantees the file is closed even if an exception is raised mid-parse — no leaked handles. Same reason you wrap instrument/SSH sessions in context managers in test code.

q: Given a log, print the worst ACLR and pass/fail against 55 dBc — how?
a: Read the file, regex-extract the ACLR numbers, take min() (higher-is-better so the worst is the smallest), compare to 55 with any tolerance, return PASS/FAIL. Guard the empty case. That's the evaluate_aclr function above.
tags: automation python rct measurements kpi resume

q: What is a pytest fixture and why use one?
a: A fixture provides reusable setup/teardown injected into tests by name. The code before yield runs before the test (connect the analyzer), the code after runs as teardown (close it) even on failure. Scope (function/session) controls how often it runs — session-scope to connect the instrument once for the whole run.

q: How do you run the same test across 4 bandwidths without copy-paste?
a: @pytest.mark.parametrize with a list of (bw, limit) tuples — pytest generates one test case per tuple, each reported separately, so one failing BW doesn't hide the others.

q: Robot Framework vs pytest — when would you pick Robot?
a: Robot is keyword-driven and reads almost like English, so it suits large mixed-skill teams sharing reusable keyword libraries and gives rich HTML reports out of the box (my Mavenir work). pytest is code-first and better when tests need real Python logic (the ruauto RCT suites). Both can drive the same UEs/instruments via libraries.

q: How do you make a data-driven test in Robot?
a: Use [Template] on the test case pointing at a keyword; each row of arguments below it becomes one iteration — e.g. an attach/detach cycle repeated N times, or the same measurement across bands.

q: What does *OPC? do and why query it?
a: *OPC? (operation complete) blocks until the instrument finishes the pending command and returns 1. You query it after RST/CONFig/trigger so you don't FETCh a result before the sweep/measurement is actually done — otherwise you read stale or partial data.
tags: automation python lab instruments measurements resume

q: How do you run traffic on 10 UEs at once in Python?
a: Address each UE by its ADB serial (adb -s), then launch the per-UE work concurrently with a ThreadPoolExecutor (threads are fine here because the work is I/O-bound — waiting on adb/iperf, not CPU). Collect per-UE results and aggregate. For CPU-bound work you'd use multiprocessing instead.

q: Write a function to find the reference sensitivity by binary search.
a: Bracket the power [lo, hi]; test the midpoint; if the miss-detection rate is within limit the UE still decodes so search lower, else search higher; stop when the range is under your resolution. That's find_sensitivity above — O(log range) instead of a linear sweep (and it mirrors the real PRACH/sensitivity search, see PRACHDM01).

q: Why is a set the right tool for "first duplicate"?
a: Membership testing in a set is O(1) average, so one pass over the stream is O(n). Using a list and 'in' would be O(n) per check → O(n²). Same reasoning behind using a set for detected-preamble bookkeeping.

q: Walk me through what happens end-to-end when the RSSI-accuracy test runs.
a: test_Rx_RSSI_Accuracy declares the sheet/columns/frequencies and returns them; the road-trip driver loops antenna×freq, selects the antenna and restarts L1/L2, and calls configure_test_Rx_RSSI_Accuracy. That computes setup-loss/EIRP/TRP math, reads the RU model to pick the calibration offset, loads the ETM1.1 UL waveform, then sweeps SG power in a U-aware three-phase controller. At each power _measure reads PHY rct_stats once and N samples of RU-CLI RSSI + BLER, averages them, records PHY−CLI, and writes a row. At the end _rssi_acc_report builds the xlsx + BLER/RSSI graphs and interpolates the 5% BLER sensitivity.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: Why compare CLI RSSI against PHY RSSI at all — aren't they the same number?
a: No — they come from different subsystems. The CLI get-rssi is what the operator/EMS sees (post-calibration, per-ADC), the PHY rct_stats is L1's internal estimate. If they diverge, either the RU's RSSI calibration/offset is wrong or the reporting path is broken. The test characterises that gap across the full power range, so a calibration error shows up as a consistent PHY−CLI diff.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: Why is BLER high at BOTH the top and bottom of the power sweep?
a: At the top the ADC saturates/clips (input above full-scale), so the samples are distorted and decode fails; at the bottom the signal drops into the noise floor and SINR collapses. In between there's a clean ~0% valley. That U-shape is exactly why the sweep first descends to find the clean region before hunting the low-power knee — otherwise you'd mistake the saturated top for the sensitivity edge.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: You read the PHY once per power step but the CLI N times — why the asymmetry?
a: The PHY value comes from tailing l1_Debug.log inside the phynode container, which only rewrites every few seconds. The N CLI reads complete in milliseconds, so reading the PHY per sample would just return N identical values plus N wasted docker round-trips. One PHY read per step, mirrored across the sample rows, is correct and much faster.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: How do you go from "logical antenna 2" to the right RSSI number in the CLI output?
a: get-rssi prints one line per physical ADC. A per-band mapping table (adc_mappings[fhgw_band][band][antenna_index]) translates the logical antenna to the physical ADC index — on the 5-band AAU, B28 antenna 0 is ADC 4, not ADC 0 — then I regex that line for adc_dbfs and rssi. Wrong mapping = you silently report a different antenna's power.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: What's EIRP vs TRP here, and where does the +3/+6 dB come from?
a: EIRP at the RU input = generator power + external_gain (which is −setup_loss, the cable/path loss). TRP adds the splitter correction: the low bands (B8/B28) feed through a 2:1 splitter (+3 dB) and the mid bands (B1/B3)/B41 through a 4:1 (+6 dB), so TRP = EIRP + that correction. It's derived from the band, with a config override.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: How would you extend this test to a new band or RU model?
a: Almost no code — add the band's ADC layout to adc_mappings, add the frequencies to the cadence, and populate rssi_model_offsets[model][fhgw_band][band][ant] in fdd_test_setup.json. The sweep, averaging, PHY/CLI reads and report are band-agnostic; only the mapping and calibration tables are data.
tags: automation rct features measurements rssi sensitivity resume deepdive

q: If PHY−CLI diff is, say, 3 dB and constant across power, what do you conclude?
a: A constant offset points to a calibration/offset error in the RU's RSSI reporting (or a wrong rssi_model_offsets entry) — not a linearity problem. A diff that grows toward the top would suggest compression/clipping; one that grows at the bottom suggests a noise-floor/SINR issue. Constant → fix the offset table; power-dependent → investigate the analog/ADC front-end.

q: Name the main RAN KPI categories and one KPI in each.
a: Accessibility (RRC/E-RAB setup success), Retainability (call/session drop rate), Mobility (handover success rate), Integrity (DL/UL throughput, latency, BLER), Availability (cell availability), and Utilisation (PRB utilisation) — plus voice KPIs like VoLTE drop rate. Each maps to a counter ratio and a set of degradation causes.
tags: notes kpi lte 5g measurements troubleshooting debug

q: Accessibility KPI dropped in a cell — how do you troubleshoot?
a: Split it: RRC setup success (RACH/preamble, congestion, admission) vs E-RAB setup success (core/transport, QoS, licensing). Check RACH counters and preamble/MSG failures, PRB/CPU load, admission-control rejects (ARP), and S1/NG transport. Correlate with RSRP/SINR to rule out coverage.
tags: notes kpi lte 5g measurements troubleshooting debug

q: Trace a signal end-to-end through the radio transceiver — transmit and receive.
a: TX: digital baseband → DAC → baseband/IF filter → variable gain/attenuator → I/Q modulator → up-conversion mixer (×LO → RF) → driver + Power Amplifier (last active stage, delivers output power) → duplexer/filter → antenna. RX: antenna → duplexer/filter → LNA (first stage — sets system Noise Figure) → down-conversion mixer (×LO → IF/baseband) → filter → AGC → ADC → digital baseband. Boundaries to name: DAC/ADC = digital↔analog; PA last on TX, LNA first on RX (Friis: the first stage dominates cascade NF).

q: What are the UE identities in LTE and how many digits does each have?
a: IMSI = 15 digits (MCC 3 + MNC 2–3 + MSIN). IMEI = 15 (device). IMEISV = 16 (IMEI + 2-digit software version). GUTI / S-TMSI = temporary identities used on air after first attach for privacy so the IMSI is not sent in the clear.

q: Explain LTE authentication (the request/response) and how it maps to 5G / AUSF.
a: EPS-AKA (4G): the MME fetches auth vectors from the HSS (RAND, AUTN, XRES, KASME). It sends RAND + AUTN to the UE (the auth request). The USIM verifies AUTN and computes RES (the auth response). The MME checks RES == XRES → authenticated. 5G map: MME→AMF, HSS→AUSF + UDM/ARPF (AUSF is the 5G authentication server), IMSI→SUPI carried encrypted as SUCI. Note: AUSF is a 5G function — in 4G it is the MME+HSS doing AKA.

q: In which SIB are the cell-reselection parameters carried? (LTE and NR)
a: LTE: SIB3 = serving + intra-freq reselection common (q-Hyst, s-IntraSearch, threshServing); SIB4 = intra-freq neighbour list (+ blacklist); SIB5 = inter-freq carriers + reselection. (SIB2 is common radio resource config — RACH/PUCCH/PUSCH/power/timers — NOT reselection.) NR renumbers it: SIB2 = reselection common, SIB3 = intra-freq, SIB4 = inter-freq. Remember both: LTE 3/4/5, NR 2/3/4.

q: How does the source eNB know which target eNB to send the X2 Handover Request to?
a: The UE's A3 measurement report carries the target PCI (and its ECGI if configured). The source resolves PCI → target eNB/cell via its Neighbour Relation Table / ANR, which corresponds to an X2 link set up beforehand (X2 Setup earlier exchanged each eNB's served-cell info: PCI, ECGI, TAC, PLMN, EARFCN). The HO Request then goes over that X2AP association. Key point: X2 + ANR must pre-exist before any handover.

q: What vital information is carried in the X2 Handover Request and Handover Request Acknowledge?
a: HANDOVER REQUEST (source→target): target ECGI, GUMMEI, UE-AMBR, the E-RAB list (E-RAB ID + QoS: QCI/ARP/GBR-MBR + S-GW UL GTP-TEID), UE security caps + KeNB* + NCC, and the Source→Target transparent container (UE RRC context, meas config, C-RNTI). HANDOVER REQUEST ACK (target→source): admitted E-RABs (+ DL/UL forwarding TEIDs) and the Target→Source transparent container = the RRCConnectionReconfiguration with mobilityControlInfo (target PCI/EARFCN, new C-RNTI, dedicated RACH preamble, T304). The two transparent containers are the crux of the answer.

q: A UE has low throughput — what do you check, layer by layer?
a: Work down the stack: RF — RSRP/RSRQ/SINR/CQI; PHY — MCS & rank (MIMO layers), BLER/HARQ retransmissions; MAC — RB allocation / scheduler, buffer status; features — CA (are all CCs active?), TM mode, UL/DL & TDD split; transport — S1/X2 / GTP / backhaul congestion; endpoints — UE category cap, TCP window / MTU; environment — interference / PCI collision / noise floor. Correlate PHY KPIs up through MAC to transport rather than guessing.

q: Walk the VoLTE call flow.
a: Voice over IMS over LTE bearers: UE attaches and gets a default bearer QCI 5 to the IMS APN (SIP signalling) → IMS registration (SIP REGISTER via P-CSCF/S-CSCF, IMS-AKA) → SIP INVITE + SDP codec negotiation → a dedicated bearer QCI 1 (GBR, conversational voice) is set up for the RTP media → call connects and voice flows on QCI 1. If LTE coverage is lost mid-call, SRVCC hands the voice leg to 3G/2G CS.

q: Have you worked on test automation? (asked when you had not yet)
a: Be honest — a senior interviewer sees through a bluff in two follow-ups: "I can read and modify code and write some, but I hadn't built automation." Then show growth: "since then I've built pytest and Robot-Framework patterns, SCPI/pyvisa instrument control, and traced a full RCT feature (RSSI accuracy) in code." Honesty + evidence of learning beats overclaiming. (See the Automation tab, AUTO01–AUTO08.)
